relationship: close narrative counterpart to Babylon's siege setting
rationale: The oracle is situated while Nebuchadnezzar and his forces fight Jerusalem and Judah's cities. The closing account dates Nebuchadnezzar's investment of Jerusalem and describes the siege lasting into Zedekiah's eleventh year; it supplies a particular counterpart for the Jerusalem part of that setting.
source_text: The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord while Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, his whole army, and all the land under his rule were fighting Jerusalem and all Judah’s cities:

target_units.text: In the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, on the tenth of the month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and all his force came against Jerusalem. They enclosed her with a palisade and built around her with squared stones.
The city was under siege until the eleventh year of King Zedekiah.

relationship: close threatened burning and subsequent account of Jerusalem's burning
rationale: The message to Zedekiah predicts that Babylon's king will seize and burn the city. The closing narrative records Nebuzaradan's arrival and the burning of the Lord's house, the royal house and the city's houses.
source_text: Thus said the Lord: Go to Zedekiah king of Judah and tell him, Thus said the Lord: This city will certainly be handed over to Babylon’s king. He will seize it and burn it with fire.

target_units.text: In the fifth month, on the tenth of the month, Nebuzaradan, the chief guard who stood before the king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem.
He burned the Lord’s house, the king’s house, and all the city’s houses; every great house he burned with fire.

relationship: close repeated prediction of Zedekiah's encounter with Babylon's king
rationale: Both oracles deny Zedekiah's escape, describe his mouth and eyes meeting those of Babylon's king, and announce his entry into Babylon. The uncommon paired mouth-and-eye language makes the correspondence particularly close.
source_text: You will certainly not be saved from his hand. You will certainly be captured and handed over to him. Your eyes will see his eyes, and his mouth will speak with your mouth. You will enter Babylon.

target_units.text: Zedekiah will certainly not be saved from the Chaldeans’ hand, but will certainly be handed over to Babylon’s king. His mouth will speak to his mouth, and his eyes will see his eyes.
Zedekiah will enter Babylon and remain there.

relationship: contrast between promised and denied royal lament
rationale: Zedekiah is promised mourning with the lament O lord. The oracle naming Jehoiakim denies mourning and the corresponding Alas, lord lament. The distinct kings receive opposite predictions about this public expression of royal honor.
source_text: You will die in peace. As they wept for your fathers who reigned before you, they will weep for you and lament you, O lord! For I have spoken the word, said the Lord.

target_units.text: Therefore thus says the Lord concerning Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah: Woe upon this man! They will certainly not mourn him, O brother! Nor will they weep for him, Alas, lord!

relationship: related named fortified cities of Judah
rationale: Jeremiah identifies Lachish and Azekah among the fortified cities still resisting. Chronicles lists Lachis and Azeka among Rehoboam's walled and supplied cities. The passages give related fortification settings under different kings; their supplied spellings are preserved.
source_text: while Babylon’s king’s force fought Jerusalem and Judah’s cities, Lachish and Azekah; these were the fortified cities left among Judah’s cities.

target_units.text: Adoraim, Lachis, and Azeka,
Saraa, Aialon, and Chebron, which belongs to Judah and Benjamin—walled cities.
He fortified them with walls and placed leaders in them, with supplies of food, oil, and wine.

relationship: parallel solemn undertaking to end oppression within the community
rationale: Zedekiah concludes a covenant to proclaim release. Nehemiah's assembly promises restitution, swears before priests and carries out its undertaking. The comparison concerns a publicly pledged remedy for oppression; the later reversal in Jeremiah contrasts with Nehemiah's reported compliance.
source_text: The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord after King Zedekiah concluded a covenant with the people to proclaim release:

target_units.text: They said, “We will return it and ask nothing from them. We will do as you say.” I called the priests and made them swear to act according to this word.

I shook out my wrap and said, “So may God shake out from his house and his labor every man who does not uphold this word. So shall he be shaken out and empty.” All the assembly said, “Amen,” and praised the Lord. The people carried out this word.

relationship: close legal counterpart for freeing Hebrew male and female slaves
rationale: Jeremiah specifies release of both Hebrew male and female slaves. Deuteronomy explicitly provides for a Hebrew man or woman to serve six years and then be sent free; its stated service term is supplied by the law, rather than asserted in this individual source unit.
source_text: each was to send his Hebrew male slave and his Hebrew female slave away free, so that a man from Judah would not be enslaved.

target_units.text: And if your brother, a Hebrew man or a Hebrew woman, is sold unto you, he shall serve you six years; and in the seventh year you shall send him forth free from you.

relationship: contrast between reversing and fulfilling an undertaking of restitution
rationale: The covenant participants turn back from their undertaking to release their slaves. Nehemiah records an oath of restitution and says the people carried out the word. The neighboring source unit explains the reversal as renewed enslavement.
source_text: All the magnates and all the people who had entered the covenant to send away their male and female slaves turned back,

target_units.text: They said, “We will return it and ask nothing from them. We will do as you say.” I called the priests and made them swear to act according to this word.

I shook out my wrap and said, “So may God shake out from his house and his labor every man who does not uphold this word. So shall he be shaken out and empty.” All the assembly said, “Amen,” and praised the Lord. The people carried out this word.

relationship: parallel condemnation of enslaving fellow Judeans after release
rationale: The people thrust the released servants back into slavery. Nehemiah condemns selling Jewish brothers while he and his companions have been buying brothers out of foreign bondage. Both expose conduct that reverses liberation within the community.
source_text: and thrust them into the position of male and female slaves.

target_units.text: and said to them, “We have bought our Jewish brothers who were being sold to the nations, of our own free will. And are you selling your brothers?” They fell quiet and found no answer.

relationship: close grounding of emancipation obligations in rescue from Egypt
rationale: The Lord recalls establishing the covenant when He rescued the fathers from Egypt's house of slavery. The emancipation law likewise grounds its command in Israel's former slavery and the Lord's redemption from Egypt.
source_text: Thus said the Lord, Israel’s God: I established a covenant with your fathers on the day I rescued them from Egypt, from the house of slavery, saying:

target_units.text: And you shall remember that you were a household slave in the land of Egypt, and the Lord your God redeemed you thence; therefore I command you to do this thing.

relationship: close repetition of the six-year Hebrew-servant release law
rationale: The oracle states that the Hebrew brother serves six years and must be sent free when those years are complete. Deuteronomy gives the same service term and expressly names the seventh year as the time of release; Jeremiah adds the charge that the fathers did not obey.
source_text: When six years are complete, you must send away your Hebrew brother who is sold to you. He will work for you six years, and you must send him away free. But they did not obey Me or incline their ears.

target_units.text: And if your brother, a Hebrew man or a Hebrew woman, is sold unto you, he shall serve you six years; and in the seventh year you shall send him forth free from you.

relationship: parallel public covenant before the Lord at His house
rationale: Jeremiah recalls a covenant made before God in the house bearing His name. Kings describes a king and people at the Lord's house covenanting to uphold the written commandments. The commitments have different immediate contents, but share the public sanctuary setting and obligation before God.
source_text: Today they turned to do what was right before My eyes, each proclaiming his neighbor’s release. They concluded a covenant before Me in the house over which My name is invoked.

target_units.text: The king went up to the Lord’s house, with every man of Judah and all who inhabited Jerusalem, the priests, the prophets, and all the people, from small to great. He read in their hearing all the words of the covenant book found in the Lord’s house.

The king stood beside the pillar and made a covenant before the Lord: to follow the Lord and keep His commandments, testimonies, and ordinances with the whole heart and whole soul, upholding the words of this covenant, the things written in this book. All the people stood in the covenant.

relationship: related profanation of God's name through faithless solemn commitment
rationale: Reversing the promised release is explicitly called profaning God's name. Leviticus joins unjust swearing by that name with its profanation. Jeremiah concerns the covenant just made before God; the law addresses unjust use of His name in an oath.
source_text: Then you reversed yourselves and profaned My name by bringing back your male and female slaves, whom you had sent away free in their own persons, to be your slaves.

target_units.text: And you shall not swear by My name for an unjust cause, and you shall not profane the name of your God. I am the Lord your God.

relationship: close covenant judgment through sword, death and bread scarcity
rationale: The ironic proclamation of release hands the covenant breakers over to sword, death and famine. Leviticus describes the sword exacting the covenant's penalty, death among the people, surrender to enemies and scarcity of bread.
source_text: Therefore thus said the Lord: You did not obey Me by proclaiming release, each to his neighbor. So I proclaim release for you to sword, death, and famine! I will give you over to scattering among all the earth’s kingdoms.

target_units.text: And I will bring upon you a sword exacting the penalty of the covenant. You shall flee into your cities, and I will send death among you; you shall be handed into enemies’ hands.
When I afflict you with a scarcity of bread, ten women shall bake your bread in one oven and give back your bread by weight. You shall eat and in no wise be filled.

relationship: close covenant-curse language of scattering among earthly kingdoms
rationale: Jeremiah announces scattering among all the earth's kingdoms. Deuteronomy uses the same worldwide-kingdom scattering language in its curse of defeat before enemies, giving a specific counterpart to this part of Jeremiah's judgment.
source_text: Therefore thus said the Lord: You did not obey Me by proclaiming release, each to his neighbor. So I proclaim release for you to sword, death, and famine! I will give you over to scattering among all the earth’s kingdoms.

target_units.text: The Lord give you over to slaughter before your enemies. You shall go forth by one way against them, and you shall flee by seven ways before them; and you shall be scattered among all the kingdoms of the earth.

relationship: close covenant curse of corpses feeding birds and beasts
rationale: Both passages consign the dead to the birds of heaven and beasts of the earth. Deuteronomy additionally says no one will drive the creatures away; Jeremiah applies the threat to the covenant breakers.
source_text: I will hand them over to their enemies, and their carcasses will become food for the birds of heaven and the wild beasts of the earth.

target_units.text: And your dead shall be food for the birds of heaven, and for the beasts of the earth; and there shall be none to drive them away.

relationship: close threatened surrender and narrated capture of Zedekiah
rationale: The first clause promises to hand Zedekiah and the rulers to their enemies. The closing account describes Zedekiah's capture, judgment and removal to Babylon. This connection concerns that named royal surrender and does not resolve the source's unusual subsequent clause about the fleeing force.
source_text: I will hand Zedekiah king of Judea and their rulers over to their enemies. And the force of Babylon’s king is for those running away from them.

target_units.text: and the Chaldean force pursued the king and overtook him beyond Jericho. All his servants scattered away from him.
They captured the king and brought him to the king of Babylon at Deblatha, and he spoke to him in judgment.
The king of Babylon slaughtered Zedekiah’s sons before his eyes, and he slaughtered all Judah’s rulers at Deblatha.
He blinded Zedekiah’s eyes and bound him in fetters. The king of Babylon brought him to Babylon and put him in a mill house until the day he died.

relationship: close explanation of the returning force that will burn Jerusalem
rationale: The Lord promises to bring the force back to seize and burn the land's cities. The later oracle places the Chaldeans' withdrawal in the setting of Pharaoh's advance and then predicts their return to seize and burn Jerusalem.
source_text: I am giving orders, says the Lord, and will bring them back to this land. They will fight against it, take it, and burn it with fire, along with Judah’s cities; I will make them deserted of inhabitants.

target_units.text: Pharaoh’s force came out of Egypt. The Chaldeans heard the report about them and withdrew from Jerusalem.
The Lord’s word came to Jeremiah:
Thus said the Lord: Tell Judah’s king, who sent to you to seek Me, Pharaoh’s force, which came out to help you, will return to Egypt’s land.
The Chaldeans themselves will return, fight this city, seize it, and burn it with fire.

relationship: related identification of Jonadab son of Rechab
rationale: The family names Jonadab son of Rechab as the father who commanded its abstinence. Kings independently names Jonadab son of Rechab meeting Jehu and joining his chariot. The target identifies the named figure without supplying the wine command itself.
source_text: They said, We certainly will not drink wine, because Jonadab son of Rechab, our father, commanded us: Neither you nor your sons must ever drink wine.

target_units.text: He went from there and found Jonadab son of Rechab on the road coming to meet him, and blessed him. Jehu said to him, ‘Is your heart upright with my heart, as my heart is with your heart?’ Jonadab said, ‘It is.’ Jehu said, ‘If it is, give me your hand.’ He gave his hand, and he brought him up to himself onto the chariot.
He said to him, ‘Come with me and see me being zealous for the Lord Sabaoth.’ He seated him in his chariot.

relationship: related wine abstinence under different binding commitments
rationale: The Rechabites refuse wine because of their father's enduring command. Numbers requires abstinence from wine and vine products during a consecration vow. The comparison concerns commanded abstinence; it does not classify the Rechabites as the vow-takers described in Numbers.
source_text: They said, We certainly will not drink wine, because Jonadab son of Rechab, our father, commanded us: Neither you nor your sons must ever drink wine.

target_units.text: Speak unto the sons of Israel, and you shall say unto them: If a man or woman solemnly vows a vow of consecration unto the Lord, to be set apart

from wine and strong drink, he shall be purified from wine. He shall drink neither vinegar of wine, nor vinegar of strong drink, nor anything prepared from grapes; and he shall eat neither fresh grapes nor raisins.
All the days of his vow he shall consume nothing made from the vine: wine, from pressed grape skins unto the seed.

relationship: parallel tent dwelling as sojourners in a land
rationale: The ancestral command requires tent dwelling rather than settled houses and cultivation in the land where the family spends its time. Hebrews describes Abraham living as a foreigner in the promised land, dwelling in tents with Isaac and Jacob. It does not impose the Rechabites' particular prohibitions on those patriarchs.
source_text: You must not build a house or sow seed, and you must not have a vineyard. You must live in tents all your days, so that you may live many days on the land where you spend your time.

target_units.text: By faith he lived as a foreigner in the land of the promise as in a foreign land, dwelling in tents with Isaac and Jacob, fellow heirs of the same promise.

relationship: related obedience to a parental command
rationale: The descendants report that their entire households have kept Jonadab's command against wine. Colossians calls children to obey their parents in all things. Jeremiah gives an ancestral family practice; the letter states the household exhortation rather than that particular abstinence rule.
source_text: We have obeyed the voice of Jonadab our father by not drinking wine all our days, we, our wives, our sons, and our daughters,

target_units.text: Children, obey your parents in all things, for this is well pleasing in the Lord.

relationship: related parental obedience with a promise of life in the land
rationale: The family says it has obeyed and done everything its father commanded, including the tent dwelling previously connected with long life. Ephesians joins obedience and honoring parents with the promise of living long upon the earth.
source_text: We lived in tents, obeying and doing everything Jonadab our father commanded us.

target_units.text: Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right.
“Honor your father and mother”—which is the first commandment with a promise—
“so that it may be well with you and you may live long upon the earth.”

relationship: related flight to Jerusalem before an invading force
rationale: The Rechabites explain their move into Jerusalem as escape from the Chaldean and Assyrian forces. Jeremiah's earlier warning calls people to gather into walled cities and flee to Zion before the northern calamity. The target supplies a comparable refuge response, without naming both forces in this source.
source_text: When Nebuchadnezzar invaded the land, we said, Come in, let us enter Jerusalem to escape the Chaldean force and the Assyrian force. So we were living there.

target_units.text: Announce in Judah, and let it be heard in Jerusalem; say: Signal with a trumpet over the land, and cry loudly! Say: Gather, and let us enter the walled cities!
Take up and flee to Zion; hurry, do not stand still, for I am bringing evils from the north and great crushing.

relationship: close refusal to hear and accept instruction
rationale: The question asks whether Judah and Jerusalem will accept discipline and hear God's words. The composite target describes the nation as neither hearing the Lord's voice nor accepting instruction, stating the same two failures directly.
source_text: Thus says the Lord: Go and say to the people of Judah and Jerusalem’s inhabitants, Will you really not accept discipline and hear My words?

target_units.text: And you will say this word to them: This is the nation that did not hear the Lord’s voice or accept instruction; faithfulness failed from their mouth.

relationship: parallel appeal from honor of a human father to honor due God
rationale: Jonadab's descendants keep his word while Judah refuses God's repeated speech. Malachi argues from a son's honor for his father to the honor God should receive as Father. Both use ordinary filial allegiance to expose failure toward God.
source_text: The sons of Jonadab son of Rechab upheld the word he commanded his children, not to drink wine, and they drank none. Yet I spoke to you from early morning and kept speaking, and you did not listen.

target_units.text: “A son honors his father, and a slave his master. If I am a father, where is My honor? If I am a master, where is the fear of Me?” says the Lord Almighty. You priests who belittle My name! But you said, “How have we belittled Thy name?”

relationship: close repeated appeal to turn from evil and foreign gods
rationale: Both passages describe God sending His servants the prophets, calling each person to turn from evil practices, promising dwelling in the ancestral land and forbidding service to other gods. Their specific cluster of commands and assurances closely corresponds.
source_text: I sent you My servants the prophets, saying, Each of you, turn from his evil way and improve your practices. Do not follow other gods to serve them, and you will live on the land I gave you and your fathers. But you did not incline your ears or listen.

target_units.text: and I was sending My servants the prophets to you, sending from early morning, and you did not listen or attend with your ears,
saying: Turn, each from his evil way and from your evil practices, and you will dwell upon the land I gave to you and your fathers from age to age.
Do not follow foreign gods to serve them and bow down to them, so that you do not provoke Me by your hands’ works into harming you.

relationship: related contrast between obeying and failing a father's command
rationale: Jeremiah contrasts the Rechabites' obedience to their father with the people's failure to obey God. Jesus' two-child parable distinguishes the child who actually does the father's will from the one who does not. The target emphasizes action rather than an identical family or historical episode.
source_text: The sons of Jonadab son of Rechab upheld their father’s command, but this people did not obey Me.

target_units.text: But what do you think? A man had two children. He came to the first and said, ‘Child, go work in the vineyard today.’
He answered, ‘I do not want to,’ but afterward he changed his mind and went.
He came to the second and said the same. He answered, ‘I will, sir,’ but did not go.
Which of the two did the father’s will?” They said, “The first.” Jesus said to them, “Truly I tell you that tax collectors and prostitutes go ahead of you into the kingdom of God.

relationship: close judgment on Jerusalem after rejection of God's words
rationale: Both declarations bring upon Jerusalem the calamities previously spoken against it. The earlier courtyard oracle explicitly grounds the judgment in refusal to hear; the Rechabite comparison immediately supplies that refusal in the source's setting.
source_text: Therefore thus said the Lord: I am bringing upon Judah and Jerusalem’s inhabitants all the calamities I pronounced against them.

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I am bringing upon this city, all its towns, and its villages all the evils I spoke against it, because they hardened their necks so as not to listen to My words.

relationship: related honoring of obedience to parental instruction
rationale: The source grounds the following favorable promise in the descendants' obedience to their father's command. Proverbs urges attention to parental discipline and presents it as a crown and collar of honor. The rewards have different forms, while parental instruction is honored in both.
source_text: Therefore thus said the Lord: Because the sons of Jonadab son of Rechab obeyed their father’s command, doing as their father commanded them,

target_units.text: Listen, son, to your father’s discipline, and do not reject your mother’s ordinances,
for you will receive a crown of graces for your head and a golden collar around your neck.

relationship: close promise that a family's man will not fail before God
rationale: The Rechabites receive a promise that a man of their family will not fail to stand before God. Solomon recalls the promise that a man of David's family will not be removed from before God on Israel's throne, subject to the stated obedience condition. The families and the royal office are distinct.
source_text: there will certainly never fail a man from the sons of Jonadab son of Rechab standing before Me all the earth’s days.

target_units.text: Now, Lord, the God of Israel, keep for Thy servant David my father what Thou didst promise him: ‘A man of yours shall not be removed from before Me sitting on Israel’s throne, if only your children guard their ways, walking before Me as you have walked before Me.’

relationship: close shared fourth-year dating under Jehoiakim
rationale: Both introductions date a word to Jeremiah to the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah. This is a precise chronological correspondence, without asserting that every word of the two literary settings was delivered on the same occasion.
source_text: In the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, the Lord’s word came to me:

target_units.text: The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all Judah’s people in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah,

relationship: parallel divine command to preserve prophetic words in writing
rationale: Jeremiah is told to put the delivered oracles on a writing roll. Isaiah is told to write on a tablet and in a book for enduring witness. The commanded written preservation is shared, while the specified media and scope differ.
source_text: Take a writing roll and write on it all the words I have delivered to you as oracles concerning Jerusalem, Judah, and all the nations, from the day I spoke to you, from the days of Josiah king of Judah until today.

target_units.text: Now then, sit and write these things on a tablet and in a book, because these things will endure for days of appointed times and for ever.

relationship: close hope that hearing warning will bring repentance and mercy
rationale: Both passages use perhaps they will hear and turn from an evil way as the hoped-for response to a warning. The source speaks of mercy toward injustices and sins; the target speaks of ceasing from the planned calamities.
source_text: Perhaps Judah’s house will hear all the calamities I intend to bring upon them, so that they turn from their evil way and I may be merciful toward their injustices and sins.

target_units.text: Perhaps they will hear and turn, each from his evil way, and I will cease from the evils I plan to do to them because of their evil practices.

relationship: close corroborating notice of Baruch writing from Jeremiah's mouth
rationale: The source names Baruch son of Neriah writing the Lord's words from Jeremiah's mouth. The later notice again identifies Baruch writing words in the scroll from Jeremiah's mouth and dates the setting to Jehoiakim's fourth year.
source_text: Jeremiah called Baruch son of Neriah, and he wrote on a writing roll, from Jeremiah’s mouth, all the Lord’s words which He had delivered to him as oracles.

target_units.text: The word Jeremiah the prophet spoke to Baruch son of Neriah when he wrote these words in the scroll from Jeremiah’s mouth, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah king of Judah:

relationship: related restriction of Jeremiah's movement by royal confinement
rationale: Jeremiah explains that being under guard prevents his entry into the Lord's house. The target describes Zedekiah shutting him in the royal prison court. These are distinct dated settings of the same prophet's confinement; the target does not identify the source's unspecified place of custody.
source_text: Jeremiah instructed Baruch, I am under guard and cannot enter the Lord’s house.

target_units.text: The king of Babylon’s force had built siegeworks against Jerusalem, and Jeremiah was kept in the prison court at the king’s house.
King Zedekiah had shut him in there, saying, Why do you prophesy, saying, Thus said the Lord: I am handing this city over to Babylon’s king, and he will take it?

relationship: parallel public reading of sacred words in an assembly fasting before God
rationale: Baruch must read the roll publicly at the Lord's house on a fast day. Nehemiah describes an assembly fasting, confessing and reading God's law. The source is prophetic warning and the target is the law book, rather than the same document.
source_text: Read from this roll in the people’s hearing at the Lord’s house on a fast day, and read it to all Judah’s people coming from their city.

target_units.text: On the twenty-fourth day of this month, the sons of Israel assembled with fasting and in sackcloth.
The sons of Israel separated themselves from every foreigner. They stood and confessed their sins and the lawless deeds of their fathers.
They stood in their places and read from a book of the law of the Lord their God. They confessed to the Lord and worshiped the Lord their God.

relationship: parallel prayer and turning from evil in hope of mercy
rationale: Jeremiah hopes an appeal for mercy and turning from evil will follow the reading amid threatened wrath. God's answer concerning the temple in Chronicles joins prayer, seeking Him and turning from wicked ways with forgiveness and healing of the land.
source_text: Perhaps their appeal for mercy will fall before the Lord, and they will turn from their evil way, for great are the Lord’s wrath and anger which He has pronounced against this people.

target_units.text: and if My people, upon whom My name has been invoked, are ashamed, and pray, and seek My face, and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven, and be propitious toward their sins, and heal their land.

relationship: parallel reading a sacred document in the people's hearing
rationale: Baruch performs the instructed public reading of the Lord's words from the document. Nehemiah describes Esdras reading the law while the people's ears attend to it. Both identify the reader, written text and listening assembly.
source_text: Baruch did everything Jeremiah instructed him, reading the Lord’s words from the document in the Lord’s house.

target_units.text: and read from it from the hour when the sun gave light until midday, before the men and women, who were understanding; the ears of all the people were directed toward the book of the law.

relationship: parallel assembly of the people for a solemn fast
rationale: Jeremiah dates a gathering of Jerusalem and Judah for a fast before the Lord to Jehoiakim's eighth year and ninth month. Joel calls for a consecrated fast and gathered congregation. The target supplies no matching year or month.
source_text: In King Jehoiakim’s eighth year, in the ninth month, all the people in Jerusalem and Judah’s house assembled for a fast before the Lord.

target_units.text: Blow a trumpet in Zion! Consecrate a fast; proclaim a service.
Gather the people; consecrate the congregation. Choose elders; gather infants nursing at breasts. Let the bridegroom leave his bedroom and the bride her bridal chamber.

relationship: close public reading of divine words at the Lord's house
rationale: Baruch reads Jeremiah's words in the Lord's house in all the people's hearing. Kings describes the king reading the covenant book to Judah, Jerusalem, priests, prophets and people at that house. The settings closely correspond while readers and documents differ.
source_text: Baruch read Jeremiah’s words from the document in the Lord’s house, in the house of Gemariah son of Shaphan the scribe, in the upper court at the entrance of the New Gate of the Lord’s house, in all the people’s hearing.

target_units.text: The king went up to the Lord’s house, with every man of Judah and all who inhabited Jerusalem, the priests, the prophets, and all the people, from small to great. He read in their hearing all the words of the covenant book found in the Lord’s house.

relationship: parallel official report bringing a sacred document to royal attention
rationale: Micaiah reports to the rulers the words he heard Baruch read. Kings describes Sapphan bringing the book to Josiah, reporting its discovery and reading it before him. These are distinct stages of official transmission, not an assertion that the named messengers are the same person.
source_text: Micaiah reported to them all the words he had heard when Baruch read in the people’s hearing.

target_units.text: He brought it to King Josiah, reported to the king, and said, ‘Your servants have melted down the silver found in the Lord’s house and given it into the hand of the workers appointed in the Lord’s house.’
Sapphan the scribe told the king, ‘Chelkias the priest gave me a book.’ Sapphan read it before the king.

relationship: same-chapter contrast in reception of the prophetic roll
rationale: The rulers request that Baruch read the roll again to them. The king later cuts and burns it as Jehudi reads its columns. The two audiences' responses to the same written prophecy form a concrete literary contrast.
source_text: They said to him, Read it again to us. Baruch read it.

target_units.text: When Jehudi read three or four columns, the king cut them off with the scribe’s knife and threw them into the fire on the brazier, until the whole roll was consumed in the brazier’s fire.

relationship: related named writers transmitting another speaker's message
rationale: Baruch identifies Jeremiah's oral report as what he wrote down. Tertius identifies himself as the writer of Romans, whose opening names Paul. The source expressly describes dictation; the target identifies the letter's writer without specifying that writing process.
source_text: Baruch said, Jeremiah reported all these words to me from his mouth, and I wrote them in a document.

target_units.text: I, Tertius, who wrote the letter, greet you in the Lord.

relationship: parallel concealment of prophets threatened by royalty
rationale: The rulers tell Jeremiah and Baruch to hide and keep their whereabouts unknown. Kings describes Obadiah hiding the Lord's prophets when Jezebel was killing them. The particular common action is protective concealment under a royal threat.
source_text: They said to Baruch, Go and hide, you and Jeremiah. Let no one know where you are.

target_units.text: When Jezebel was striking the Lord’s prophets, Obadiah took a hundred men who were prophets, hid them fifty to a cave, and sustained them with bread and water.

relationship: parallel reading a recovered religious document before a king
rationale: Jehudi fetches the deposited roll and reads it to the king and the surrounding rulers. Sapphan reports the discovered law book and reads it before Josiah. Their different royal responses become explicit in the surrounding narratives.
source_text: The king sent Jehudi to fetch the roll. He took it from Elishama’s house, and Jehudi read it to the king and all the rulers standing around him.

target_units.text: Sapphan the scribe told the king, ‘Chelkias the priest gave me a book.’ Sapphan read it before the king.

relationship: same-chapter destruction of a scroll followed by its replacement
rationale: Jehoiakim cuts and burns the roll until it is consumed. The later command and fulfillment restore all its words in another roll, with additional words. The connection shows that destruction of the physical document does not end the announced message.
source_text: When Jehudi read three or four columns, the king cut them off with the scribe’s knife and threw them into the fire on the brazier, until the whole roll was consumed in the brazier’s fire.

target_units.text: Take another roll again and write all the words that were on the roll which King Jehoiakim burned.
Say, Thus said the Lord: You burned this roll, saying, Why did you write in it that Babylon’s king will certainly enter and destroy this land, and people and animals will cease from it?
Therefore thus said the Lord concerning Jehoiakim king of Judah: He will have no one sitting on David’s throne. His carcass will be thrown out in the day’s heat and the night’s frost.
I will visit him, his family, and his servants, and bring upon them, Jerusalem’s inhabitants, and Judah’s land all the calamities I pronounced to them, but they did not listen.
Baruch took another roll and wrote on it, from Jeremiah’s mouth, all the words of the document Jehoiakim burned. Still more words like these were added to it.

relationship: contrast between unresponsive and repentant royal hearing
rationale: Jehoiakim and his servants neither seek anything nor tear their garments upon hearing the words. Josiah tears his garments and orders inquiry of the Lord after hearing the law book. The comparison preserves the source's stated actions without substituting an unstated description of fear.
source_text: Neither the king nor his servants who heard all these words sought anything or tore their garments.

target_units.text: When the king heard the words of the book of the law, he tore his garments.
The king commanded Chelkias the priest, Achikam son of Sapphan, Achobor son of Michaias, Sapphan the scribe, and Asaia the king’s servant:

‘Come, seek the Lord for me, for all the people, and for all Judah concerning the words of this book that has been found. For great is the Lord’s anger which burns among us, because our fathers did not listen to this book’s words, to do everything written against us.’

relationship: related royal rejection of warning counsel
rationale: The named rulers advise Jehoiakim not to burn the roll, against the burning already described. Amaziah rejects a prophet's counsel and is told that his refusal brings destruction. The advisers and the matters of counsel differ; the connection concerns disregarded royal warning.
source_text: Elnathan, Gedaliah, and Gemariah advised the king not to burn the roll.

target_units.text: While he was speaking to him, the king said, “Have I appointed you the king’s counselor? Take care that you are not flogged.” The prophet fell silent, but said, “I know that He has purposed against you to destroy you, because you have done this and have not heeded my counsel.”

relationship: parallel hidden prophetic servants escaping a royal threat
rationale: Jehoiakim orders Jeremiah and Baruch arrested, but they are hidden. Obadiah hides prophets during Jezebel's attacks. Jeremiah's unit does not name the agent of concealment, whereas Kings expressly names Obadiah.
source_text: The king ordered Jerahmeel the king’s son and Seraiah son of Azriel to arrest Baruch and Jeremiah. But they were hidden.

target_units.text: When Jezebel was striking the Lord’s prophets, Obadiah took a hundred men who were prophets, hid them fifty to a cave, and sustained them with bread and water.

relationship: parallel command to replace destroyed writing with its former words
rationale: Jeremiah is commanded to take another roll and write the words of the burned roll. Moses is commanded to prepare replacement tablets on which God will write the words of the shattered tablets. The media, writers and circumstances of destruction differ.
source_text: Take another roll again and write all the words that were on the roll which King Jehoiakim burned.

target_units.text: The Lord said to Moses, “Hew for yourself two tablets of stone like the first, and come up to Me on the mountain. I will write upon the tablets the words that were upon the first tablets, which you shattered.

relationship: related prophecy of destruction affecting people and livestock
rationale: The king objects to the prediction that Babylon's king will destroy the land and that people and animals will cease from it. The target threatens death to the city's people and livestock, followed by the surrender of Zedekiah and the survivors. Both announcements concern Judah's judgment, with different immediate addressees and details.
source_text: Say, Thus said the Lord: You burned this roll, saying, Why did you write in it that Babylon’s king will certainly enter and destroy this land, and people and animals will cease from it?

target_units.text: And I will strike all this city’s inhabitants, the people and the livestock, with a great death, and they will die.

And afterward—thus says the Lord—I will give Zedekiah king of Judah, his servants, and the people remaining in this city after death, famine, and sword into the hands of their enemies who seek their lives. They will cut them down with the sword’s edge. I will not spare them or have compassion on them.

relationship: close repeated judgment upon Jehoiakim's exposed corpse
rationale: Both named oracles against Jehoiakim predict his body being cast out dishonorably. Jeremiah 22 describes a donkey's burial beyond Jerusalem's gate; this source specifies exposure to daytime heat and nighttime frost.
source_text: Therefore thus said the Lord concerning Jehoiakim king of Judah: He will have no one sitting on David’s throne. His carcass will be thrown out in the day’s heat and the night’s frost.

target_units.text: Therefore thus says the Lord concerning Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah: Woe upon this man! They will certainly not mourn him, O brother! Nor will they weep for him, Alas, lord!
He will be buried with a donkey’s burial; swept up, he will be thrown beyond Jerusalem’s gate.

relationship: close announced calamities following refusal to hear
rationale: The Lord will bring the previously pronounced calamities upon the king's circle, Jerusalem and Judah because they did not listen. The courtyard oracle likewise announces the spoken calamities upon Jerusalem and its surrounding settlements because they refuse God's words.
source_text: I will visit him, his family, and his servants, and bring upon them, Jerusalem’s inhabitants, and Judah’s land all the calamities I pronounced to them, but they did not listen.

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I am bringing upon this city, all its towns, and its villages all the evils I spoke against it, because they hardened their necks so as not to listen to My words.

relationship: parallel writing after the loss of an earlier sacred document
rationale: Baruch writes the destroyed document's words again on another roll, with more words added. In the setting of replacement tablets, Exodus records writing the covenant's words. The comparison concerns renewed inscription; only Jeremiah explicitly mentions added words.
source_text: Baruch took another roll and wrote on it, from Jeremiah’s mouth, all the words of the document Jehoiakim burned. Still more words like these were added to it.

target_units.text: The Lord said to Moses, “Write these words for yourself, for according to these words I have made a covenant with you and Israel.”
Moses was there before the Lord forty days and forty nights, eating no bread and drinking no water. He wrote these words on the covenant tablets, the Ten Words.

relationship: close appointment of Zedekiah by Nebuchadnezzar with differing succession notices
rationale: Both passages name Nebuchadnezzar as the one who made Zedekiah king over Judah. Jeremiah says he reigned in place of Jehoiakim, while the preceding Chronicles unit names Jechonias; the connection concerns the explicit appointment and does not harmonize that succession difference.
source_text: Zedekiah son of Josiah reigned in place of Jehoiakim; Nebuchadnezzar had made him king over Judah.

target_units.text: At the turn of the year King Nebuchadnezzar sent and brought him into Babylon with the desirable vessels of the Lord’s house. He made Zedekiah, his father’s brother, king over Judah and Jerusalem.

relationship: close refusal of Jeremiah's divine message under Zedekiah
rationale: Jeremiah says king, servants and people did not obey the Lord's words through the prophet. Chronicles says Zedekiah felt no shame before Jeremiah and God's word, then describes the officials', priests' and people's breaches of faith. Both connect the reign with rejection of the prophetic message.
source_text: Neither he nor his servants nor the people of the land obeyed the Lord’s words, which He spoke through Jeremiah.

target_units.text: He did what was evil before the Lord his God. He felt no shame before Jeremiah the prophet, and at what came from the Lord’s mouth,
in breaking his obligations to King Nebuchadnezzar, who had made him swear by God. He hardened his neck and strengthened his heart so as not to return to the Lord God of Israel.
All the distinguished men of Judah, the priests, and the people of the land multiplied breaches of faith in the nations’ abominations and defiled the Lord’s house in Jerusalem.

relationship: close royal delegation seeking Jeremiah's intercession
rationale: Zedekiah sends men, including Zephaniah son of Maaseiah, asking Jeremiah to pray. The earlier delegation from the same king also includes that named priest and asks Jeremiah to inquire of the Lord concerning Babylon's attack. The other delegate's name differs.
source_text: King Zedekiah sent Jehucal son of Shelemiah and Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest to Jeremiah, saying, Please pray for us to the Lord.

target_units.text: The word that came from the Lord to Jeremiah when King Zedekiah sent to him Pashhur son of Malchiah and Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest, saying:
Ask the Lord about us, because Babylon’s king has come against us, whether the Lord will act according to all His wonders, so that he goes away from us.

relationship: related Egyptian military intervention and its inability to secure Judah
rationale: Pharaoh's advance causes a temporary Chaldean withdrawal in Jeremiah. Ezekiel describes the appeal to Egypt for military aid and denies a successful outcome for the covenant-breaking ruler. The target does not narrate this particular withdrawal, and the source does not claim lasting Egyptian deliverance.
source_text: Pharaoh’s force came out of Egypt. The Chaldeans heard the report about them and withdrew from Jerusalem.

target_units.text: He will revolt from him, sending his messengers to Egypt to give him horses and many people. Will he prosper? Will the one doing contrary things be rescued? Will one transgressing a covenant be saved?
As I live, says the Lord, surely in the place of the king who made him king—he who dishonored My curse-oath and transgressed My covenant—with him in the midst of Babylon he will die.
Pharaoh will not wage war against him with great power or a numerous crowd, amid siegeworks and the building of missile stations to remove lives.

relationship: parallel warning that Egyptian military help will fail
rationale: Jeremiah says the Egyptian force that came to help will return home. Isaiah rebukes reliance on Egypt's horses and chariots and says the helpers will grow weary. The common point is the failure of military confidence in Egypt, expressed through different predictions.
source_text: Thus said the Lord: Tell Judah’s king, who sent to you to seek Me, Pharaoh’s force, which came out to help you, will return to Egypt’s land.

target_units.text: Woe to those going down to Egypt for help, trusting in horses and chariots because there are many, and in horses, a very great multitude, but not trusting Israel’s Holy One or seeking God!
He Himself, wise, brought evils upon them; His word will certainly not be set aside. He will rise against evil people’s houses and against their futile hope,
an Egyptian human being and not God, horses’ flesh, with no help. The Lord will bring His hand against them; the helpers will grow weary, and all will perish together.

relationship: close repeated prediction of return, capture and burning
rationale: Both oracles say the force will return, take the city or land's cities and burn them. The source identifies the returning force as the Chaldeans; the earlier warning announces God's command bringing it back.
source_text: The Chaldeans themselves will return, fight this city, seize it, and burn it with fire.

target_units.text: I am giving orders, says the Lord, and will bring them back to this land. They will fight against it, take it, and burn it with fire, along with Judah’s cities; I will make them deserted of inhabitants.

relationship: related rejection of false assurance about Jerusalem's safety
rationale: Jeremiah forbids assuming that the Chaldeans will depart for good. The temple sermon similarly warns against confidence in words promising benefit from the temple. The false assurances differ, but both concern unfounded confidence in Jerusalem's preservation.
source_text: For thus said the Lord: Do not suppose within yourselves, The Chaldeans will flee and leave us. They certainly will not leave.

target_units.text: Do not put your confidence in yourselves on false words, because they will not benefit you at all when they say, ‘The Lord’s temple, the Lord’s temple it is.’

relationship: related defeat by a seemingly insufficient force under divine judgment
rationale: Even pierced survivors of the Chaldean force are said to be capable of burning Jerusalem. Deuteronomy asks how one or two can rout multitudes unless God has delivered His people up. Neither target supplies the other's particular military numbers or injuries.
source_text: Even if you struck the whole Chaldean force fighting you and some were left pierced through, each in his place, these would rise and burn this city with fire.

target_units.text: How shall one pursue a thousand, and two put tens of thousands to flight, unless God had sold them, and the Lord had delivered them up?

relationship: related purchase in Benjamin's land by Jeremiah
rationale: The source says Jeremiah leaves to buy from Benjamin's land. The field narrative names Anathoth in Benjamin and records his acquisition from Hanamel. The comparison identifies another explicit purchase involving the same prophet and district, without collapsing the distinct narrative settings into one event.
source_text: Jeremiah left Jerusalem to go to Benjamin’s land, to buy from there among the people.

target_units.text: Hanamel son of Shallum, your father’s brother, is coming to you, saying, Acquire my field at Anathoth for yourself, because you have the right to receive it as a possession.

Hanamel son of Shallum, my father’s brother, came to me in the prison court and said, Acquire my field in Benjamin’s land at Anathoth, because you have the right to acquire it, and you are the elder. Then I knew that this was the Lord’s word.
I acquired the field of Hanamel, my father’s brother’s son, and weighed out to him seventeen shekels of silver.

relationship: related accusation of political disloyalty met by denial
rationale: Sarouiah, the man with whom Jeremiah lodged, arrests him with the accusation of flight to the Chaldeans; Jeremiah denies it in the following unit. Nehemiah is accused of planning revolt and answers that the charge is fabricated. The allegations and accusers are different.
source_text: At Benjamin’s Gate there was a man with whom he lodged, Sarouiah son of Shelemiah son of Hananiah. He arrested Jeremiah, saying, You are fleeing to the Chaldeans!

target_units.text: In it was written: “It has been reported among the nations that you and the Jews are planning to revolt. That is why you are building the wall, and you are becoming their king.
Besides this, you have appointed prophets for yourself so that you may sit in Jerusalem as king in Judah. Now these words will be reported to the king. Come now, let us take counsel together.”
I sent to him, saying, “Nothing like these words you say has happened. You are falsely devising them from your own heart.”

relationship: parallel explicit denial of an accusation of political disloyalty
rationale: Jeremiah calls the defection charge a lie and denies fleeing to the Chaldeans. Nehemiah denies the reported rebellion and says it was devised from the accuser's heart. Jeremiah additionally reports that his denial did not prevent arrest.
source_text: He said, A lie! I am not fleeing to the Chaldeans. But Sarouiah would not listen to him; he arrested Jeremiah and brought him to the rulers.

target_units.text: I sent to him, saying, “Nothing like these words you say has happened. You are falsely devising them from your own heart.”

relationship: related episodes of Jeremiah being struck and confined
rationale: The rulers strike Jeremiah and put him into Jonathan's house as a prison. The earlier account describes Pashhur striking him and placing him in a trap at the Lord's house. The responsible authorities and forms of confinement remain distinct.
source_text: The rulers were embittered against Jeremiah. They struck him and sent him into the house of Jonathan the scribe, which they had made into a prison house.

target_units.text: And Pashhur son of Immer, the priest who had been appointed leader of the Lord’s house, heard Jeremiah prophesying these words.
And he struck him and put him into the trap, which was at the gate of the separated upper house that was in the Lord’s house.

relationship: close repeated royal confrontation over the prediction of captivity
rationale: Zedekiah secretly asks whether there is a word from the Lord and receives the prediction of surrender to Babylon's king. The prison-court account likewise presents Zedekiah confronting Jeremiah over the oracle that city and king will be handed over and the king will enter Babylon.
source_text: Zedekiah sent and summoned him. The king secretly asked him whether there was a word from the Lord. He said, There is. You will be handed over to Babylon’s king.

target_units.text: King Zedekiah had shut him in there, saying, Why do you prophesy, saying, Thus said the Lord: I am handing this city over to Babylon’s king, and he will take it?
Zedekiah will certainly not be saved from the Chaldeans’ hand, but will certainly be handed over to Babylon’s king. His mouth will speak to his mouth, and his eyes will see his eyes.
Zedekiah will enter Babylon and remain there.

relationship: parallel protest of confinement despite no wrong done
rationale: Jeremiah asks what wrong he has committed to warrant imprisonment. Joseph says he has done nothing yet has been cast into the pit. The source is a question to the king and the target an assertion to the cupbearer, not the same judicial episode.
source_text: Jeremiah said to the king, How have I wronged you, your servants, or this people, that you are putting me in prison?

target_units.text: “For I was indeed stolen from the land of the Hebrews; and here I have done nothing, yet they have cast me into this pit.”

relationship: related exposure of optimistic prophecy about Babylon
rationale: Jeremiah challenges the prophets who said Babylon's king would not come against the land. The target identifies Hananiah as a false prophet and records his promise that Babylon's yoke is smashed and deportees and vessels will return. These are distinct optimistic claims, not identical quoted predictions.
source_text: Where are your prophets who prophesied to you, saying, Babylon’s king certainly will not come against this land?

target_units.text: And in the fourth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the fifth month, Hananiah son of Azzur, the false prophet from Gibeon, said to me in the Lord’s house before the priests and all the people:
Thus said the Lord: I smashed Babylon’s king’s yoke.
In two full years I will return to this place the vessels of the Lord’s house,
and Jeconiah and Judah’s deportees, because I will smash Babylon’s king’s yoke.

relationship: close later repetition of Jeremiah's prison appeal
rationale: Jeremiah asks not to be returned to Jonathan's house to die. In the later secret-interview narrative the king instructs him to report precisely that appeal. The target records the proposed report, while the source gives the appeal itself.
source_text: Now, lord king, let my appeal for mercy fall before you. Why send me back to Jonathan the scribe’s house—and will I not die there?

target_units.text: tell them, I am casting my appeal for mercy before the king’s eyes, not to send me back to Jonathan’s house to die there.

relationship: related provision of bread to prophets under threat
rationale: Jeremiah receives a daily loaf during confinement until the city's supply fails. Obadiah supplies hidden prophets with bread and water during Jezebel's attacks. The protectors and confinement settings differ, while food sustains endangered prophetic servants in both.
source_text: The king gave orders, and they put him into the prison house, giving him one loaf a day from outside where they bake, until the city’s loaves ran out. Jeremiah remained in the prison court.

target_units.text: When Jezebel was striking the Lord’s prophets, Obadiah took a hundred men who were prophets, hid them fifty to a cave, and sustained them with bread and water.

relationship: close repeated choice between remaining to die and surrendering to live
rationale: Both oracles say that remaining in the city brings death by sword and famine, while going out to the Chaldeans preserves life. The source calls life one's gain, while the target calls it spoil; both frame survival as what the surrendering person obtains.
source_text: Thus said the Lord: Whoever remains in this city will die by sword and famine. Whoever goes out to the Chaldeans will live; his life will be his gain, and he will live.

target_units.text: Whoever stays in this city will die by sword and famine; whoever goes out to join the Chaldeans who have shut you in will live, and his life will be spoil, and he will live.

relationship: close repeated prediction of the city's surrender to Babylon
rationale: Both declarations say Jerusalem will be handed over to Babylon's king. The target additionally specifies burning by fire and God's adverse purpose; those details are not added to this shorter source unit.
source_text: For thus said the Lord: This city will certainly be handed over to the force of Babylon’s king, and he will seize it.

target_units.text: Because I have fixed My face upon this city for evils and not for good things. It will be handed into Babylon’s king’s hands, and he will burn it down with fire.

relationship: parallel accusation that a prophet's adverse words endanger the nation
rationale: Jeremiah's opponents tell the king that his words weaken fighters and people and deliver evil rather than peace. Amaziah tells Jeroboam that Amos conspires against him and that the land cannot endure his words of death and captivity. Both accusations portray unwelcome prophecy as a political danger.
source_text: They said to the king, Let that man be killed! By speaking these words to them he weakens the hands of the fighters left in the city and of all the people. This man delivers oracles of evil to this people, not peace.

target_units.text: Amaziah, priest of Bethel, sent to Jeroboam king of Israel, saying, “Amos is forming conspiracies against you in the midst of Israel’s house. The land certainly cannot endure all his words,
because Amos says, ‘Jeroboam will die by a sword, and Israel will be led captive away from its land.’”

relationship: parallel ruler yielding a prisoner's fate to hostile demand
rationale: Zedekiah puts Jeremiah in the accusers' hands; the account says the king was unable to oppose them. Luke describes the accusers' voices prevailing and Pilate handing Jesus over to their will. The rulers' stated motives and the resulting punishments differ.
source_text: The king said, He is in your hands—for the king was unable to oppose them.

target_units.text: But they pressed him with loud voices, demanding that He be crucified, and their voices prevailed.
And Pilate decided that their demand should be granted.
He released the man who had been thrown into prison for uprising and murder, whom they were demanding; but he handed Jesus over to their will.

relationship: close narrative parallel of being cast into a waterless pit
rationale: Jeremiah is lowered into a pit without water, where there is mire. Joseph is stripped and cast into an empty pit explicitly having no water. The shared waterless-pit confinement is specific; Genesis does not supply Jeremiah's mire.
source_text: They threw him into the pit of Malchiah the king’s son in the prison court and lowered him into the pit. There was no water in it, only mire, and he was in the mire.

target_units.text: And when Joseph came to his brothers, they stripped Joseph of the tunic of many colours which was upon him.
And they took him and cast him into the pit; and the pit was empty, having no water.

relationship: close later divine address to the named Ethiopian rescuer
rationale: The source introduces Ebed-melech the Ethiopian as hearing of Jeremiah's confinement. The later oracle names the same Ethiopian and promises preservation amid the city's calamity because he trusted God. The intervening source narrative supplies his act of intervention.
source_text: Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, who was in the king’s house, heard that they had put Jeremiah in the pit. The king was at Benjamin’s Gate.

target_units.text: Go and tell Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, Thus said the Lord, Israel’s God: I am bringing My words upon this city for calamity, not good.
I will save you that day and certainly will not hand you over to the men you fear.
I will certainly save you. You certainly will not fall by the sword; your life will be your gain because you trusted in Me, says the Lord.

relationship: related advocacy for a vulnerable person's just treatment
rationale: Ebed-melech confronts the king over the treatment that threatens Jeremiah with death from hunger. Proverbs calls for speaking, judging justly and deciding the case of the poor and weak. The comparison concerns intervention for a vulnerable person, without assigning Jeremiah a lifelong economic status.
source_text: You have acted wickedly in what you did, killing this man through hunger, for there are no more loaves in the city.

target_units.text: Open your mouth and judge justly, and decide the case of the poor and weak.

relationship: parallel command to rescue someone facing death
rationale: The king orders Ebed-melech to bring Jeremiah out of the pit so that he does not die. Proverbs commands rescuing those led to death and ransoming those being killed. The source gives a particular intervention, including thirty men, rather than those details being supplied by the proverb.
source_text: The king instructed Ebed-melech, Take thirty men from here under your command and bring him up from the pit so that he does not die.

target_units.text: Rescue those being led to death, and ransom those being killed; do not hold back.

relationship: close imagery of rescue from a pit and muddy confinement
rationale: Jeremiah is pulled out of the pit whose mire was described earlier. The psalm praises God for bringing the speaker out of a pit of misery and muddy slime. The source names a physical rescue by ropes; the comparison does not identify the psalmist with Jeremiah or the two passages as one event.
source_text: They pulled him with the ropes and brought him up from the pit. Jeremiah remained in the prison court.

target_units.text: He brought me up from a pit of misery and from muddy slime; He set my feet upon a rock and directed my steps.

relationship: parallel demand that the recipient of a divine word conceal nothing
rationale: Zedekiah tells Jeremiah to hide no word from him. Eli similarly asks Samuel what was spoken and insists that no word be hidden; Samuel reports it all. The addressees and settings differ, while the demand for complete prophetic disclosure closely corresponds.
source_text: The king sent and summoned him to himself, to the aselisi house in the Lord’s house. The king said to him, I will ask you something. Please hide no word from me.

target_units.text: He said, “What was the word spoken to you? Do not hide it from me. May God do these things to you, and add these things, if you hide from me a word of all the words spoken to you in your ears.”
Samuel reported all the words and hid nothing from him. Eli said, “He is the Lord. He will do what is good before Him.”

relationship: related danger of giving a king unwelcome prophecy
rationale: Jeremiah fears death if he answers and says the king will not heed counsel. Micaiah's adverse vision prompts the king's complaint that he prophesies only bad things. The surrounding target account later imprisons Micaiah; it does not say that the king kills him.
source_text: Jeremiah said to the king, If I tell you, will you not certainly put me to death? And if I advise you, you certainly will not listen to me.

target_units.text: Micaiah said, “Not so! I have seen all Israel scattered on the mountains like a flock without a shepherd. The Lord said, ‘These have no master. Let each return to his own house in peace.’”
The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat king of Judah, “Did I not tell you that this man prophesies no good things for me, only bad things?”

relationship: close royal oath by the living Lord not to kill a threatened servant
rationale: Zedekiah swears by the living Lord that he will not kill Jeremiah or hand him to the men. Saul likewise swears, As the Lord lives, that David will not die. The source additionally describes the Lord as the maker of their life.
source_text: The king swore to him, As the Lord lives, who made this life for us, I will not kill you or hand you over to these men.

target_units.text: Saul listened to Jonathan’s voice, and Saul swore, saying, “As the Lord lives, he shall not die.”

relationship: close application of the surrender-and-life promise to the king
rationale: The source tells Zedekiah that going out to Babylon's commanders will preserve his life and household and prevent the city's burning. The earlier oracle offers life to anyone going out to the Chaldeans. Jeremiah here applies the same surrender condition to the king with further consequences for household and city.
source_text: Jeremiah said to him, Thus said the Lord: If you go out to Babylon’s king’s commanders, your life will be spared and this city will certainly not be burned with fire. You and your household will live.

target_units.text: Whoever stays in this city will die by sword and famine; whoever goes out to join the Chaldeans who have shut you in will live, and his life will be spoil, and he will live.

relationship: close threatened surrender and burning of Jerusalem
rationale: The source warns that refusal to go out will leave the city to Chaldean capture and fire. The target likewise announces its handover to Babylon's king and burning. The source expressly frames that outcome against the preceding offered alternative.
source_text: But if you do not go out, this city will be handed over to the Chaldeans and they will burn it with fire. You certainly will not be saved.

target_units.text: Because I have fixed My face upon this city for evils and not for good things. It will be handed into Babylon’s king’s hands, and he will burn it down with fire.

relationship: related fear of people contrasted with trust in God
rationale: Zedekiah fears being handed to Judean deserters and mocked. Proverbs describes people being tripped up by fear and shame before others, contrasting them with the person who trusts in the Lord. The following source answer offers divine reassurance; the proverb does not name these deserters.
source_text: The king said to Jeremiah, I am concerned about the Judeans who have fled to the Chaldeans, lest they hand me over to them and mock me.

target_units.text: having feared and felt shame before people, they were tripped up; but one who trusts in the Lord will rejoice. Impiety gives a man a fall; but one who trusts in the Master will be saved.

relationship: parallel contrast between hearing God for good and refusing Him unto harm
rationale: Jeremiah urges the king to hear the Lord's word so that it will be better for him and his life spared. Isaiah joins willing hearing with the land's good things and unwilling refusal with the sword. The immediate promised benefits differ, but the contrast of responses is shared.
source_text: Jeremiah said, They certainly will not hand you over. Hear the Lord’s word which I speak to you, and it will be better for you; your life will be spared.

target_units.text: If you are willing and listen to Me, you will eat the land’s good things.
But if you are unwilling and do not listen to Me, a sword will devour you, for the Lord’s mouth has spoken these things.”

relationship: close betrayal by those formerly described as peaceful allies
rationale: The women say the king's peaceful friends deceived him and will overpower him; they also describe those friends turning away. Obadiah says covenant allies and men at peace oppose and prevail over the addressee and set ambushes. Both expose trusted peaceful relationships becoming hostile; Obadiah does not use the source's slippery-feet wording.
source_text: All the women left in Judah’s king’s house were being brought out to Babylon’s king’s rulers. They said, Your peaceful friends deceived you and will overpower you. They will bring your feet to rest in slippery places; they turned away from you.

target_units.text: All the men of your covenant sent you out as far as your borders; the men at peace with you opposed you and prevailed over you. They set ambushes beneath you. There is no understanding in them.

relationship: close prediction and narrative counterpart of royal capture and city burning
rationale: The oracle predicts the king's seizure and Jerusalem's burning, alongside the removal of his household. The closing narrative records his capture and the subsequent burning of the houses. It gives additional details of his sons' deaths and his blinding rather than repeating the source's whole household prediction.
source_text: They will bring your wives and children out to the Chaldeans. You certainly will not be saved, for Babylon’s king will seize you, and this city will be burned.

target_units.text: and the Chaldean force pursued the king and overtook him beyond Jericho. All his servants scattered away from him.
They captured the king and brought him to the king of Babylon at Deblatha, and he spoke to him in judgment.
The king of Babylon slaughtered Zedekiah’s sons before his eyes, and he slaughtered all Judah’s rulers at Deblatha.
He blinded Zedekiah’s eyes and bound him in fetters. The king of Babylon brought him to Babylon and put him in a mill house until the day he died.
In the fifth month, on the tenth of the month, Nebuzaradan, the chief guard who stood before the king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem.
He burned the Lord’s house, the king’s house, and all the city’s houses; every great house he burned with fire.

relationship: close prescribed report of an earlier prison appeal
rationale: The king tells Jeremiah to report his plea not to return to Jonathan's house to die. The earlier account records Jeremiah making that appeal. The source supplies what is to be told to the rulers, while the target contains the direct petition to the king.
source_text: tell them, I am casting my appeal for mercy before the king’s eyes, not to send me back to Jonathan’s house to die there.

target_units.text: Now, lord king, let my appeal for mercy fall before you. Why send me back to Jonathan the scribe’s house—and will I not die there?

relationship: close end of confinement followed by removal from the prison court
rationale: Jeremiah remains in the prison court until Jerusalem is taken. The subsequent account records his removal from that court and delivery to Gedaliah, after which he lives among the people. The connection traces the stated endpoint of his confinement without supplying an unstated exact release date.
source_text: Jeremiah remained in the prison court until the time Jerusalem was captured.

target_units.text: They sent and took Jeremiah from the prison court and handed him over to Gedaliah son of Ahikam son of Shaphan. They brought him out, and he lived among the people.

relationship: close parallel dating of Nebuchadnezzar's siege
rationale: Both accounts place Nebuchadnezzar's arrival with his force against Jerusalem in Zedekiah's ninth year and tenth month. The closing account additionally supplies the tenth day and describes the enclosing works.
source_text: In the ninth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and his whole force arrived against Jerusalem and besieged it.

target_units.text: In the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, on the tenth of the month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and all his force came against Jerusalem. They enclosed her with a palisade and built around her with squared stones.

relationship: close parallel breach of Jerusalem at the siege's end
rationale: The source dates the breach to Zedekiah's eleventh year and the ninth day of the fourth month. The closing account gives the eleventh-year end of the siege, the ninth day and the breach, but does not repeat the fourth-month designation in those units.
source_text: In Zedekiah’s eleventh year, on the ninth day of the fourth month, the city was breached.

target_units.text: The city was under siege until the eleventh year of King Zedekiah.
On the ninth of the month, the famine grew severe in the city, and there were no loaves for the people of the land.

The city was breached, and all the warriors went out at night by the gate between the wall and the outer wall beside the king’s garden, while the Chaldeans surrounded the city. They went by the road to Arabah,

relationship: related foreign rulers occupying Jerusalem's gates
rationale: The Babylonian commanders enter and sit at the Middle Gate. The opening oracle predicts northern kingdoms setting their thrones at Jerusalem's gate forecourts. The narrative supplies a particular gate occupation, without expressly calling the commanders' seats thrones.
source_text: All Babylon’s king’s commanders entered and sat at the Middle Gate: Nargalasar, Samagoth, Nabousachar, Nabousaris, Nagargasnaser Rabamag, and the remaining commanders of Babylon’s king.

target_units.text: Because behold, I am summoning all the kingdoms from the north of the land, says the Lord. They will come and each set his throne at the forecourts of Jerusalem’s gates, against all her surrounding walls and against all Judah’s cities.

relationship: close linked accounts of Jeremiah's release and residence with Gedaliah
rationale: The source records Jeremiah being removed from the prison court, handed to Gedaliah and living among the people. The next account describes release from handcuffs, permission to return to Gedaliah and residence with him at Mizpah. The distinct custody details are preserved rather than collapsed.
source_text: They sent and took Jeremiah from the prison court and handed him over to Gedaliah son of Ahikam son of Shaphan. They brought him out, and he lived among the people.

target_units.text: Behold, I have released you from the handcuffs on your hands. If it seems good to you to come with me to Babylon, come, and I will look after you.

But if not, go off and return to Gedaliah son of Ahikam son of Shaphan, whom Babylon’s king appointed in Judah’s land, and live with him among the people in Judah’s land. Go wherever it seems good in your eyes to go. The chief guard gave him gifts and sent him away.
He came to Gedaliah at Mizpah and lived among the people left in the land.

relationship: close identification of the Ethiopian addressed after rescuing Jeremiah
rationale: The oracle addresses Ebed-melech the Ethiopian in the setting of the city's coming calamity. The preceding chapter identifies him by the same name and origin and narrates his intervention to bring Jeremiah out of the pit. This supplies the recipient's particular narrative background.
source_text: Go and tell Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, Thus said the Lord, Israel’s God: I am bringing My words upon this city for calamity, not good.

target_units.text: Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, who was in the king’s house, heard that they had put Jeremiah in the pit. The king was at Benjamin’s Gate.
He went out to him, spoke to the king, and said:
You have acted wickedly in what you did, killing this man through hunger, for there are no more loaves in the city.
The king instructed Ebed-melech, Take thirty men from here under your command and bring him up from the pit so that he does not die.
Ebed-melech took the men and entered the king’s underground house. He took old rags and old ropes from there and threw them down to Jeremiah in the pit.
He said, Put these beneath the ropes. Jeremiah did so.
They pulled him with the ropes and brought him up from the pit. Jeremiah remained in the prison court.

relationship: related divine assurance of rescue to one who trusts
rationale: Ebed-melech is promised deliverance from the men he fears; the following source unit grounds the promise in his trust. The psalm promises rescue and presence in affliction to one who hopes in God. It is not an identification of the psalm's beneficiary with Ebed-melech.
source_text: I will save you that day and certainly will not hand you over to the men you fear.

target_units.text: Because he hoped in Me, I will rescue him; I will shelter him, because he knew My name.
He will call upon Me, and I will hear him; I am with him in affliction, and I will take him out and glorify him.

relationship: close personal promises that preserved life will be one's gain
rationale: Both assurances promise life as gain amid announced calamity. This source addresses Ebed-melech and explicitly grounds rescue in trust; the later oracle addresses Baruch while warning him against seeking great things for himself.
source_text: I will certainly save you. You certainly will not fall by the sword; your life will be your gain because you trusted in Me, says the Lord.

target_units.text: Are you seeking great things for yourself? Do not seek them, for I am bringing calamities upon all flesh, says the Lord. I will give your life as gain wherever you walk.

relationship: related notices of Jeremiah being released from custody
rationale: The source introduces the chief guard's release of Jeremiah from handcuffs among the deportees. The preceding narrative records his removal from the prison court and placement with Gedaliah. The comparison concerns the named prophet's liberation and does not replace the native Daman wording with another place-name.
source_text: The word that came from the Lord to Jeremiah afterward, after Nebuzaradan, the chief guard from Daman, sent him away, when he took him in handcuffs among Judah’s exiles who were being led to Babylon.

target_units.text: They sent and took Jeremiah from the prison court and handed him over to Gedaliah son of Ahikam son of Shaphan. They brought him out, and he lived among the people.

relationship: related acknowledgment of calamity previously announced against the city
rationale: The chief guard acknowledges that the Lord spoke the calamities against the place. Jeremiah's earlier oracle explicitly announces the city's surrender to Babylon's king and burning. The target supplies a specific earlier announcement rather than words quoted verbatim by the guard.
source_text: The chief guard took him and said to him, The Lord your God spoke these calamities against this place.

target_units.text: Because I have fixed My face upon this city for evils and not for good things. It will be handed into Babylon’s king’s hands, and he will burn it down with fire.

relationship: close explanation of national calamity as covenant disobedience
