rationale: The guard says the Lord acted because the people sinned and did not obey His voice. Deuteronomy explains judgment on the land and removal to another land by abandonment of God's covenant and service to other gods. Both attribute the disaster to disobedience, with Deuteronomy specifying its idolatrous form.
source_text: And the Lord acted, because you sinned against Him and did not obey His voice.

target_units.text: And they shall say, Because they forsook the covenant of the Lord, the God of their fathers, which He made with their fathers when He brought them forth out of the land of Egypt;
and they went and served other gods, and bowed down unto them, whom they did not know, and whom He had not allotted unto them.
And the Lord was kindled in wrath against that land, to bring upon it all the curses which are written in this book of the law.
And the Lord removed them from their land in wrath, and anger, and exceeding great indignation, and cast them into another land, as it is now.

relationship: close parallel appointment of a governor over Judah's remnant
rationale: Jeremiah's account names Gedaliah son of Ahikam son of Shaphan as Babylon's king's appointee in Judah. Kings names Godolias son of Achikam son of Saphan in the same governing role over the people left in the land. The source additionally gives Jeremiah permission to live with him; the supplied name forms remain distinct in the quotations.
source_text: But if not, go off and return to Gedaliah son of Ahikam son of Shaphan, whom Babylon’s king appointed in Judah’s land, and live with him among the people in Judah’s land. Go wherever it seems good in your eyes to go. The chief guard gave him gifts and sent him away.

target_units.text: As for the people remaining in Judah’s land whom Nabouchodonosor king of Babylon had left, he appointed over them Godolias son of Achikam son of Saphan.

relationship: related residence and assembly at the governor's settlement
rationale: Jeremiah comes to Gedaliah at Mizpah and lives among those remaining. Kings describes the military commanders coming to Godolias at Massephath. The target supplies another gathering around the governor; it does not itself mention Jeremiah's residence.
source_text: He came to Gedaliah at Mizpah and lived among the people left in the land.

target_units.text: All the commanders of the force, they and their men, heard that the king of Babylon had appointed Godolias. They came to Godolias at Massephath: Ishmael son of Nathanias, Joanan son of Karee, Saraias son of Thanemath the Netophathite, and Jezonias son of the Machathi, they and their men.

relationship: close parallel report of the governor's appointment reaching the commanders
rationale: Both accounts describe Babylon's king appointing a governor over the remaining population and the commanders hearing of the appointment. Jeremiah additionally specifies the entrusted men and wives who had not been deported.
source_text: All the commanders of the force in the countryside, they and their men, heard that Babylon’s king had appointed Gedaliah in the land and had entrusted to him men and their wives whom he had not deported to Babylon.

target_units.text: As for the people remaining in Judah’s land whom Nabouchodonosor king of Babylon had left, he appointed over them Godolias son of Achikam son of Saphan.

All the commanders of the force, they and their men, heard that the king of Babylon had appointed Godolias. They came to Godolias at Massephath: Ishmael son of Nathanias, Joanan son of Karee, Saraias son of Thanemath the Netophathite, and Jezonias son of the Machathi, they and their men.

relationship: close parallel lists of commanders coming to the appointed governor
rationale: Both accounts list Ishmael, Johanan or Joanan, Seraiah or Saraias, and Jezaniah or Jezonias among those coming with their men to the governor. The supplied patronymics and the placement of the Netophathite description differ; the comparison does not make the lists identical.
source_text: Ishmael son of Nethaniah, Johanan son of Kareah, Seraiah son of Tanhumeth, the sons of Ophe the Netophathite, and Jezaniah son of the Maacathite came to Gedaliah at Mizpah, they and their men.

target_units.text: All the commanders of the force, they and their men, heard that the king of Babylon had appointed Godolias. They came to Godolias at Massephath: Ishmael son of Nathanias, Joanan son of Karee, Saraias son of Thanemath the Netophathite, and Jezonias son of the Machathi, they and their men.

relationship: close parallel oath urging settlement and service to Babylon's king
rationale: Both speeches reassure the commanders and their men concerning the Chaldeans and urge remaining in the land and serving Babylon's king for their good. Jeremiah says the Chaldeans' servants, whereas Kings says the passing of the Chaldeans; that wording difference is preserved.
source_text: Gedaliah swore to them and their men, saying, Do not be afraid of the Chaldeans’ servants. Live in the land and work for Babylon’s king, and it will be better for you.

target_units.text: Godolias swore to them and their men and said, ‘Do not fear the passing of the Chaldeans. Settle in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it shall go well for you.’

relationship: related counsel to sustain settled life under Babylonian rule
rationale: Gedaliah tells the remnant to gather produce, store it and inhabit their towns while he stays at Mizpah. The letter to the deportees instructs building houses, planting gardens, eating their produce and seeking the land's peace. The source concerns Judah's remnant and the target the deportees, not one location.
source_text: Behold, I am staying before you at Mizpah to stand before the Chaldeans who come against you. Gather wine and summer fruit, gather oil, put them in your containers, and live in the cities you have taken over.

target_units.text: Build houses and dwell in them; plant gardens and eat their fruits,
and take wives and beget sons and daughters. Take wives for your sons and give your daughters to husbands. Multiply and do not become fewer,
and seek the peace of the land where I deported you, and pray to the Lord for them, because in its peace you will have peace.

relationship: related agricultural provision after displacement
rationale: Those returning to Gedaliah gather much wine, summer fruit and oil in Judah. The exiles' letter commands planting gardens and eating their fruit. The shared feature is settled provision from produce amid displacement; the target does not report this harvest or its abundance.
source_text: They came to Gedaliah in Judah’s land at Mizpah and gathered a very great amount of wine and summer fruit, and oil.

target_units.text: Build houses and dwell in them; plant gardens and eat their fruits,

relationship: close warning of Ishmael's murderous intent followed by the attack
rationale: The commanders warn that Ishmael intends to take Gedaliah's life, although Gedaliah disbelieves them. The next chapter records Ishmael and his men attacking Gedaliah and those with him. It confirms the threatened attack without independently establishing the alleged commission from Ammon's king.
source_text: They said to him, Do you really know that Belisa king of Ammon’s people has sent Ishmael to you to take your life? But Gedaliah did not believe them.

target_units.text: In the seventh month, Ishmael son of Nethaniah son of Elasa, of the king’s family, came with ten men to Gedaliah at Mizpah. They ate bread together there.
Ishmael and the ten men with him rose and struck Gedaliah, whom Babylon’s king had appointed over the land,
and all the Judeans with him at Mizpah, and all the Chaldeans found there.

relationship: related anticipated danger to the gathered remnant and its later seizure
rationale: Johanan warns that Gedaliah's death would scatter the people gathered to him. The later narrative records Ishmael taking away the remaining people at Mizpah. This supports the particular danger to the settlement without endorsing Johanan's proposed preemptive killing or claiming it occurred.
source_text: Johanan spoke secretly to Gedaliah at Mizpah: Let me go and strike down Ishmael, and let no one know, lest he take your life and all Judah gathered to you be scattered, and Judah’s survivors perish.

target_units.text: Ishmael turned back all the people left at Mizpah and the king’s daughters whom the chief guard had entrusted to Gedaliah son of Ahikam, and he went away to the far side of Ammon’s people.

relationship: close disbelief of a warning contradicted by the ensuing assault
rationale: Gedaliah calls Johanan's report about Ishmael false and forbids action against him. The ensuing account names Ishmael as the one who rises with his men and strikes Gedaliah. The narrative outcome directly bears on the disputed warning.
source_text: Gedaliah said to Johanan, Do not do this thing, for you are speaking falsehoods about Ishmael.

target_units.text: In the seventh month, Ishmael son of Nethaniah son of Elasa, of the king’s family, came with ten men to Gedaliah at Mizpah. They ate bread together there.
Ishmael and the ten men with him rose and struck Gedaliah, whom Babylon’s king had appointed over the land,

relationship: close parallel arrival of Ishmael with ten men in the seventh month
rationale: Both accounts place Ishmael's arrival with ten men and royal-family affiliation in the seventh month. Jeremiah names the grandfather Elasa and Kings Elisama; Jeremiah additionally records eating bread together. Those details are not silently harmonized.
source_text: In the seventh month, Ishmael son of Nethaniah son of Elasa, of the king’s family, came with ten men to Gedaliah at Mizpah. They ate bread together there.

target_units.text: In the seventh month Ishmael son of Nathanias son of Elisama, of the kings’ offspring, came with ten men. He struck Godolias—who died—and the Judeans and Chaldeans who were with him at Massephath.

relationship: related treachery in a relationship of shared bread
rationale: Ishmael eats bread with Gedaliah before the attack recorded next. The psalm laments treachery by a trusted man of peace who ate the speaker's loaves. The connection concerns betrayed table fellowship, not an identification of the psalmist or its unnamed companion.
source_text: In the seventh month, Ishmael son of Nethaniah son of Elasa, of the king’s family, came with ten men to Gedaliah at Mizpah. They ate bread together there.

target_units.text: For even the man of my peace, in whom I hoped, who ate my loaves, magnified treachery against me.

relationship: close parallel attack by Ishmael and his ten companions on the governor
rationale: Both accounts describe Ishmael and ten men striking Babylon's appointed governor, named Gedaliah in Jeremiah and Godolias in Kings. Kings expressly adds that the governor died; the surrounding Jeremiah narrative likewise treats the attack as his killing.
source_text: Ishmael and the ten men with him rose and struck Gedaliah, whom Babylon’s king had appointed over the land,

target_units.text: In the seventh month Ishmael son of Nathanias son of Elisama, of the kings’ offspring, came with ten men. He struck Godolias—who died—and the Judeans and Chaldeans who were with him at Massephath.

relationship: close parallel inclusion of Judean and Chaldean victims
rationale: Jeremiah includes the Judeans with the governor at Mizpah and the Chaldeans found there among the victims. Kings likewise names Judeans and Chaldeans with the governor at Massephath. The shared victim groups are more specific than a general account of violence.
source_text: and all the Judeans with him at Mizpah, and all the Chaldeans found there.

target_units.text: In the seventh month Ishmael son of Nathanias son of Elisama, of the kings’ offspring, came with ten men. He struck Godolias—who died—and the Judeans and Chaldeans who were with him at Massephath.

relationship: related grain offering accompanied by frankincense
rationale: The mourners carry grain offerings and frankincense to the Lord's house. Leviticus prescribes a flour offering with oil and frankincense, presented to the priests. The target explains the particular offering combination; it does not supply the source's eighty men or their mourning actions.
source_text: eighty men came from Shechem, Salem, and Samaria, with shaved beards and torn clothes, beating themselves, carrying grain offerings and frankincense to bring to the Lord’s house.

target_units.text: And if a soul brings a gift as a sacrifice unto the Lord, his gift shall be fine flour; and he shall pour oil upon it, and put frankincense upon it. It is a sacrifice.

And he shall bring it unto the sons of Aaron, the priests; and when he has taken from it a full handful of the fine flour with the oil and all its frankincense, the priest shall place its memorial portion upon the altar: a sacrifice, a sweet savour unto the Lord.

relationship: related invitation or private approach preceding concealed murderous intent
rationale: Ishmael invites the approaching mourners to Gedaliah although Gedaliah is already dead; the next unit records their slaughter. Joab has Abner brought back and draws him aside to speak while lying in wait, then strikes him. The invitations and victims differ, but deceptive approach precedes killing in both.
source_text: Ishmael went out to meet them. They were walking and weeping, and he said to them, Come in to Gedaliah.

target_units.text: Joab returned from David and sent messengers after Abner. They brought him back from the well of Seiram, but David did not know.
Abner returned to Hebron. Joab took him aside beside the gate to speak with him while lying in wait, and struck him there in the loins. He died for the blood of Asahel, Joab’s brother.

relationship: close illustration of wealth serving as ransom for life
rationale: Ten men disclose stores of grain, honey and oil, and Ishmael spares them. Proverbs says a man's own wealth is the ransom of his life. The narrative supplies a particular use of valuable provisions to avert death without approving the killer's conduct.
source_text: Ten men found there said to Ishmael, Do not kill us, for we have stores in the countryside: wheat, barley, honey, and oil. He passed them by and did not kill them among their brothers.

target_units.text: A man’s own wealth is the ransom of his life, but a poor person does not face a threat.

relationship: related Asa-Baasha conflict and Asa's construction at the remnant's settlement
rationale: Jeremiah attributes the large cistern to Asa because of Baasha. Chronicles narrates their conflict and Asa's subsequent building of Gabae and Maspha from Rama's materials. It supplies the named royal conflict and construction background but does not mention this cistern or establish its particular dimensions.
source_text: The cistern into which Ishmael threw all those he had struck down is a large cistern that King Asa made because of Baasha king of Israel. Ishmael filled it with the slain.

target_units.text: In the thirty-eighth year of Asa’s reign, Baasha king of Israel came up against Judah and fortified Rama, to allow no exit or entrance for Asa king of Judah.
Asa took gold and silver from the treasuries of the Lord’s house and the king’s house and sent it to the son of Ader, Syria’s king, who dwelt in Damascus, saying,
“Make a covenant between me and you, and between my father and your father. Behold, I have sent you gold and silver. Come, drive Baasha king of Israel away from me, and let him depart from me.”
The son of Ader listened to King Asa and sent his army commanders against Israel’s cities. He struck Ion, Dan, Abelmain, and all Naphtali’s surrounding districts.
When Baasha heard, he gave up building Rama any further and stopped his work.
King Asa took all Judah and took Rama’s stones and timber with which Baasha had built. With them he built Gabae and Maspha.

relationship: close realization of the warned danger to Gedaliah's gathered people
rationale: Ishmael takes away the people left at Mizpah, including the king's daughters. Johanan's earlier warning feared the scattering of the people gathered to Gedaliah after his death. The target anticipates the settlement's vulnerability rather than describing every detail of the later abduction.
source_text: Ishmael turned back all the people left at Mizpah and the king’s daughters whom the chief guard had entrusted to Gedaliah son of Ahikam, and he went away to the far side of Ammon’s people.

target_units.text: Johanan spoke secretly to Gedaliah at Mizpah: Let me go and strike down Ishmael, and let no one know, lest he take your life and all Judah gathered to you be scattered, and Judah’s survivors perish.

relationship: related earlier warning by the commanders who later hear of the crimes
rationale: Johanan and his fellow commanders hear what Ishmael has done. The preceding account records their warning to Gedaliah and Johanan's attempt to prevent the threatened killing. The correspondence identifies their particular prior involvement, not merely another report of violence.
source_text: Johanan son of Kareah and all the commanders of the force with him heard of all the evils Ishmael had done.

target_units.text: They said to him, Do you really know that Belisa king of Ammon’s people has sent Ishmael to you to take your life? But Gedaliah did not believe them.
Johanan spoke secretly to Gedaliah at Mizpah: Let me go and strike down Ishmael, and let no one know, lest he take your life and all Judah gathered to you be scattered, and Judah’s survivors perish.

relationship: related military encounters beside Gibeon's water
rationale: Johanan's force finds Ishmael beside abundant water at Gibeon. Samuel locates the meeting of Abner's and Joab's forces at Gibeon's spring. These are distinct military encounters; Jeremiah does not specify that its abundant water is that same spring.
source_text: They led their entire army and went away to fight him. They found him beside abundant water at Gibeon.

target_units.text: Abner son of Ner and the servants of Ish-bosheth son of Saul went out from Mahanaim to Gibeon.

Joab son of Zeruiah and David’s servants went out from Hebron and met them together at Gibeon’s spring. They sat down, one group on this side of Gibeon’s spring and the other on that side of the spring.

relationship: parallel recovery of people taken captive
rationale: The people taken with Ishmael return to Johanan. Samuel describes David recovering the people and possessions taken by the Amalekites. The common result is recovery from captivity; the source does not narrate David's method of battle or its spoils.
source_text: they returned to Johanan.

target_units.text: David recovered everything the Amalekites had taken, and he rescued both his wives.
Nothing belonging to them was missing, from small to great, from the spoils to sons and daughters and everything they had taken from them. David brought it all back.

relationship: related flight to Ammon after an alleged Ammonite connection
rationale: Ishmael escapes to Ammon's people with eight men. The earlier warning alleges that Ammon's king sent him against Gedaliah. His destination is relevant to that allegation but is not independent proof of the king's commission.
source_text: Ishmael escaped with eight men and went away to Ammon’s people.

target_units.text: They said to him, Do you really know that Belisa king of Ammon’s people has sent Ishmael to you to take your life? But Gedaliah did not believe them.

relationship: parallel restoration of an abducted group including women
rationale: Johanan takes charge of the recovered people, including women, men and eunuchs. David recovers the captives, with his wives, sons and daughters expressly mentioned. The recovered groups are differently described; their lists and numbers are not equated.
source_text: Johanan and all the commanders of the force with him took all the people left whom he had brought back from Ishmael: men mighty in war, the women, the rest, and the eunuchs whom he brought back from Gibeon.

target_units.text: David recovered everything the Amalekites had taken, and he rescued both his wives.
Nothing belonging to them was missing, from small to great, from the spoils to sons and daughters and everything they had taken from them. David brought it all back.

relationship: close intended migration to Egypt followed by its narrated execution
rationale: The survivors stay near Bethlehem intending to enter Egypt. The later account records Johanan taking Judah's survivors into Egypt and reaching Taphnas. The target supplies the stated journey's outcome, not a different name for the source's stopping place.
source_text: They went away and stayed at Gaberoth-chamaam near Bethlehem, intending to go into Egypt,

target_units.text: Johanan and all the commanders of the force took all Judah’s survivors who had returned to live in the land:
the mighty men, the women, the little children, the king’s daughters, the people Nebuzaradan had left with Gedaliah son of Ahikam, and Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch son of Neriah.
They entered Egypt, for they had not obeyed the Lord’s voice. They entered Taphnas.

relationship: close explanation of flight to Egypt after the governor's murder
rationale: Jeremiah says the survivors fear the Chaldeans because Ishmael killed Babylon's appointed governor. Kings places the governor's killing immediately before the people and commanders enter Egypt for fear of the Chaldeans. The same sequence of murder, fear and migration is explicit.
source_text: away from the Chaldeans, for they feared them because Ishmael had struck Gedaliah, whom Babylon’s king had appointed in the land.

target_units.text: In the seventh month Ishmael son of Nathanias son of Elisama, of the kings’ offspring, came with ten men. He struck Godolias—who died—and the Judeans and Chaldeans who were with him at Massephath.
All the people, from small to great, and the commanders of the forces arose and entered Egypt, for they feared the Chaldeans.

relationship: close communal request for a prophet's intercession amid danger
rationale: Judah's few survivors ask Jeremiah to pray to the Lord his God for them. Samuel's people similarly ask him to pray to the Lord his God so that they do not die. The requests share prophetic intercession for an endangered community, without identical circumstances or numbers.
source_text: Jeremiah the prophet and said to him, Please let our appeal for mercy come before you. Pray to the Lord your God for these survivors, for few of us remain out of many, as your eyes see.

target_units.text: All the people said to Samuel, “Pray to the Lord your God for your servants, and we will certainly not die. We have added to all our sins the evil of asking a king for ourselves.”

relationship: close request that God disclose the way to follow
rationale: The people ask God to tell them the way they should go and what they should do. The psalm asks the Lord to make His ways known, teach His paths and guide the speaker in truth. One request concerns a community's immediate decision; the other is a personal prayer for guidance.
source_text: Let the Lord your God tell us the way we should go and the matter we should carry out.

target_units.text: Make Thy ways known to me, Lord, and teach me Thy paths.
Guide me into Thy truth and teach me, for Thou art God my Savior, and I waited for Thee the whole day.

relationship: parallel commitment to report the whole divine word without concealment
rationale: Jeremiah promises to tell whatever the Lord answers and hide no word. Samuel reports all the words and hides nothing from Eli. The source is a prospective commitment; the target narrates its performance in a different prophetic setting.
source_text: Jeremiah said to them, I have heard. I will pray to the Lord our God as you have said. Whatever word the Lord answers, I will tell you; I certainly will not hide a word from you.

target_units.text: Samuel reported all the words and hid nothing from him. Eli said, “He is the Lord. He will do what is good before Him.”

relationship: parallel prophetic undertaking to pray for the people
rationale: Jeremiah agrees to pray to the Lord for those requesting intercession. Samuel declares that he must not cease praying for the people and will show them the good way. This target specifically supports the intercessory undertaking, distinct from the source's promise of complete disclosure.
source_text: Jeremiah said to them, I have heard. I will pray to the Lord our God as you have said. Whatever word the Lord answers, I will tell you; I certainly will not hide a word from you.

target_units.text: As for me, may I never sin against the Lord by ceasing to pray for you. I will serve the Lord and show you the good and straight way.

relationship: parallel invocation of God as witness to a solemn undertaking
rationale: The people invoke the Lord as a righteous and faithful witness to their promise to act on His message. The covenant between Jacob and Laban explicitly invokes God as witness between them. Their obligations differ, but both place an undertaking before God's witness.
source_text: They said to Jeremiah, May the Lord be a righteous and faithful witness among us if we do not act according to every word with which the Lord sends you to us.

target_units.text: “Now therefore come, let us make a covenant, I and you, and let it be a witness between me and you.” And he said to him, “Behold, no one is with us; see, God is witness between me and you.”

relationship: close public pledge to do and obey everything God speaks
rationale: The survivors promise to obey whether the answer is good or bad. At the covenant-book reading the people likewise promise to do and obey everything the Lord has spoken. The source makes the unconditional character of its pledged response especially explicit.
source_text: Whether good or bad, we will obey the voice of the Lord our God, to whom we are sending you, so that it may be better for us, because we will obey the voice of the Lord our God.

target_units.text: He took the book of the covenant and read it in the hearing of the people. They said, “We will do and obey everything the Lord has spoken.”

relationship: close contrast between pledged obedience and subsequent refusal
rationale: The people promise obedience to whatever divine answer comes. The ensuing narrative records named leaders rejecting Jeremiah's answer and the people refusing to remain in Judah. This gives the later outcome of the particular undertaking rather than a generic warning about disobedience.
source_text: Whether good or bad, we will obey the voice of the Lord our God, to whom we are sending you, so that it may be better for us, because we will obey the voice of the Lord our God.

target_units.text: Azariah son of Maaseiah, Johanan son of Kareah, and all the men who spoke said to Jeremiah, You are lying! The Lord did not send you to us to say, Do not enter Egypt to live there.
Rather, Baruch son of Neriah is setting you against us, so that you will hand us over to the Chaldeans, to put us to death and have us deported to Babylon.
Johanan, all the commanders of the force, and all the people did not obey the Lord’s voice by remaining in Judah’s land.

relationship: close assurance of building and planting rather than destroying
rationale: Both promises use rebuilding without tearing down and planting without plucking out. The source conditions this assurance on the survivors remaining in the land; the earlier fig oracle concerns restoration of the deportees. The source's statement that God has rested from the calamities is not replaced with another expression.
source_text: If you remain in this land, I will build you up and certainly not tear you down; I will plant you and certainly not pluck you up. For I have rested from the calamities I brought upon you.

target_units.text: And I will fix My eyes upon them for good things and restore them to this land for good things. I will rebuild them and certainly not tear them down, plant them and certainly not pluck them out.

relationship: close divine reassurance of presence and rescue against feared people
rationale: The survivors are told not to fear Babylon's king because God is with them to rescue and save them. Jeremiah's commission likewise says not to fear those addressed because God is with him to rescue him. The beneficiary and immediate threat differ.
source_text: Do not fear Babylon’s king, whom you fear. Do not fear, says the Lord, for I am with you to rescue you and save you from his hand.

target_units.text: Do not fear them, because I am with you to rescue you, says the Lord.

relationship: related divine compassion and restoration
rationale: God promises mercy and return to the land. The psalm recalls His covenant mercy and granted compassion before captors, then asks for gathering from the nations. The source does not expressly make Babylon's king the agent of its promised mercy.
source_text: I will grant you mercy, have mercy on you, and return you to your land.

target_units.text: He remembered His covenant and changed His purpose according to His abundant mercy,
and granted them compassions before all who had taken them captive.
Save us, Lord our God, and gather us together from the nations, to give thanks to Thy holy name and boast in Thy praise.

relationship: close warned refusal to remain followed by recorded disobedience
rationale: The oracle frames refusal to remain in the land as refusal to obey the Lord. The later narrative explicitly says Johanan, the commanders and the people did not obey by remaining in Judah. The target records the conduct anticipated in the warning.
source_text: But if you say, We certainly will not remain in this land, so as not to obey the Lord’s voice,

target_units.text: Johanan, all the commanders of the force, and all the people did not obey the Lord’s voice by remaining in Judah’s land.

relationship: parallel misplaced hope for security in Egypt
rationale: The survivors imagine Egypt as a place without war, trumpets or hunger. Isaiah warns that seeking Pharaoh's help and Egyptian shelter will bring shame and reproach. Isaiah says its people did not ask God; Jeremiah's people asked and then reject the answer, so their procedures are not equated.
source_text: because we will enter Egypt’s land, certainly not see war or hear the trumpet’s sound or hunger for bread, and there we will live—

target_units.text: you who go down to Egypt, but they did not ask Me, to be helped by Pharaoh and sheltered by Egyptians.
For Pharaoh’s shelter will become your shame, and reproach for those trusting in Egypt.

relationship: parallel failure to escape danger by fleeing elsewhere
rationale: Sword and famine will meet the survivors in the Egypt to which they flee for safety. Amos pictures flight from a lion leading to a bear and apparent safety in a house ending in a snakebite. The source is a concrete destination warning, while the target expresses the futility of escape through images.
source_text: the sword you fear will find you in Egypt’s land, and the famine you are concerned about will catch up with you from behind in Egypt, and there you will die.

target_units.text: as when someone flees from a lion and a bear falls upon him, then leaps into his house, braces his hands upon the wall, and a snake bites him.

relationship: close repeated judgment upon those settling in Egypt
rationale: The source threatens those who set their faces toward Egypt with sword and famine. The later oracle likewise announces destruction of the Egyptian remnant through sword and famine, adding death in its comparison with Jerusalem. The source expressly includes foreigners as well as the people.
source_text: All the people and all the foreigners who set their faces toward Egypt’s land to live there will perish by sword and famine. None of them will be saved from the calamities I am bringing upon them.

target_units.text: to destroy all the survivors in Egypt, and they will fall. By sword and famine they will perish, from the least to the greatest, and become a reproach, a destruction, and a curse.
I will visit those staying in Egypt’s land as I visited Jerusalem, by sword, famine, and death.

relationship: close comparison of Egypt's coming judgment with Jerusalem's
rationale: Both announcements apply to the emigrants in Egypt a judgment corresponding to what already struck Jerusalem. The source describes wrath and a resulting curse and reproach; the target names sword, famine and death.
source_text: For thus said the Lord: As My wrath dripped upon Jerusalem’s inhabitants, so My wrath will drip upon you when you enter Egypt. You will become an untrodden place, subject to others, a curse, and a reproach, and you certainly will never see this place again.

target_units.text: I will visit those staying in Egypt’s land as I visited Jerusalem, by sword, famine, and death.

relationship: close prohibition of entering Egypt and its subsequent violation
rationale: The Lord explicitly says not to enter Egypt. The later narrative says they entered Egypt because they had not obeyed His voice and identifies Taphnas as their destination. The target supplies the specific disobedience to this command.
source_text: These are the things the Lord spoke concerning you, Judah’s survivors: Do not enter Egypt. And now know for certain

target_units.text: They entered Egypt, for they had not obeyed the Lord’s voice. They entered Taphnas.

relationship: related professed desire for God's word without doing it
rationale: Jeremiah condemns the people's request for prayer and promise to do the answer in light of their actual refusal. Ezekiel describes people eagerly gathering to hear a word from the Lord yet refusing to do it. Both distinguish an appearance of receptive listening from the response in action.
source_text: that you acted wickedly in your souls when you sent me, saying, Pray for us to the Lord, and we will do everything the Lord tells you.

target_units.text: And you, son of man, your people’s sons talk about you beside the walls and in the houses’ gateways. A man says to his brother, ‘Let us gather and hear what comes from the Lord!’
They come to you as people assemble and sit before you. They hear your words but certainly will not do them, because falsehood is in their mouth, and their heart follows defilements.
You become to them like the sound of a sweet-voiced, well-tuned psaltery. They will hear your words but certainly will not do them.

relationship: close charge of disobedience and its narrated form
rationale: Jeremiah says the people have not obeyed the voice with which the Lord sent him. The ensuing account identifies their disobedience as refusal to remain in Judah. The target specifies the action at issue in the source's accusation.
source_text: And you did not obey the Lord’s voice, with which He sent me to you.

target_units.text: Johanan, all the commanders of the force, and all the people did not obey the Lord’s voice by remaining in Judah’s land.

relationship: close repeated threat of death by sword and famine in Egypt
rationale: The source says the people will die by sword and famine in the place where they want to settle, identified as Egypt in the preceding warning. The later oracle explicitly names the remnant in Egypt and the same two instruments of death.
source_text: And now you will perish by sword and famine in the place where you want to go and live.

target_units.text: to destroy all the survivors in Egypt, and they will fall. By sword and famine they will perish, from the least to the greatest, and become a reproach, a destruction, and a curse.

relationship: related challenge to an unwelcome prophet's divine authority
rationale: The leaders call Jeremiah's message a lie and deny that the Lord sent it. Zedekiah son of Chenaanah challenges what sort of the Lord's spirit spoke in Micaiah and strikes him. The forms of opposition differ, while both dispute the claimed divine source of adverse prophecy.
source_text: Azariah son of Maaseiah, Johanan son of Kareah, and all the men who spoke said to Jeremiah, You are lying! The Lord did not send you to us to say, Do not enter Egypt to live there.

target_units.text: Zedekiah son of Chenaanah approached, struck Micaiah on the cheek, and said, “What sort of spirit of the Lord was it that spoke in you?”

relationship: contrast between alleged influence and Baruch's recorded writing role
rationale: The leaders accuse Baruch of setting Jeremiah against them. The earlier account explicitly describes Baruch writing from Jeremiah's mouth the words God had delivered to the prophet. That recorded scribal role is relevant to the allegation without independently establishing every motive attributed to Baruch here.
source_text: Rather, Baruch son of Neriah is setting you against us, so that you will hand us over to the Chaldeans, to put us to death and have us deported to Babylon.

target_units.text: Jeremiah called Baruch son of Neriah, and he wrote on a writing roll, from Jeremiah’s mouth, all the Lord’s words which He had delivered to him as oracles.

relationship: close refusal of the specific command against entering Egypt
rationale: The narrative says the commanders and people did not obey by remaining in Judah. The preceding oracle expressly forbids the survivors to enter Egypt. This is the particular divine instruction against which the conduct is measured.
source_text: Johanan, all the commanders of the force, and all the people did not obey the Lord’s voice by remaining in Judah’s land.

target_units.text: These are the things the Lord spoke concerning you, Judah’s survivors: Do not enter Egypt. And now know for certain

relationship: related movement of the survivors who had returned to Judah
rationale: Johanan takes the survivors who had returned to live in the land. The earlier account describes Judeans returning from neighboring countries to Gedaliah in Judah. It supplies the preceding return movement without asserting that its list identifies every individual now departing.
source_text: Johanan and all the commanders of the force took all Judah’s survivors who had returned to live in the land:

target_units.text: All the Judeans in Moab’s land, among Ammon’s people, in Idumea, and in all the land heard that Babylon’s king had left a remnant for Judah and appointed Gedaliah son of Ahikam over them.
They came to Gedaliah in Judah’s land at Mizpah and gathered a very great amount of wine and summer fruit, and oil.

relationship: close identification of the population entrusted to Gedaliah
rationale: Both passages name the king's daughters and the people entrusted by the chief guard to Gedaliah. The source also explicitly includes Jeremiah and Baruch; the target does not name those two among Ishmael's captives.
source_text: the mighty men, the women, the little children, the king’s daughters, the people Nebuzaradan had left with Gedaliah son of Ahikam, and Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch son of Neriah.

target_units.text: Ishmael turned back all the people left at Mizpah and the king’s daughters whom the chief guard had entrusted to Gedaliah son of Ahikam, and he went away to the far side of Ammon’s people.

relationship: close parallel account of the survivors' entry into Egypt
rationale: Both narratives describe the people and military commanders entering Egypt after the governor's murder. Kings expressly gives fear of the Chaldeans; Jeremiah stresses disobedience to God's voice and names Taphnas. The stated explanations are preserved rather than substituted for each other.
source_text: They entered Egypt, for they had not obeyed the Lord’s voice. They entered Taphnas.

target_units.text: All the people, from small to great, and the commanders of the forces arose and entered Egypt, for they feared the Chaldeans.

relationship: related Egyptian oracle settings at Taphnas and Tahpanhes
rationale: Jeremiah receives the word at Taphnas that introduces the following sign of Babylonian domination. Ezekiel names Tahpanhes in an oracle of Egypt's shattered power and captivity. The distinct supplied place-name forms are preserved, and the source introduction is not made to contain Ezekiel's darkness imagery.
source_text: The Lord’s word came to Jeremiah at Taphnas:

target_units.text: At Tahpanhes the day will grow dark when I shatter Egypt’s scepters there and the arrogance of her strength perishes there. A cloud will cover her, and her daughters will be led away captive.

relationship: parallel public material sign interpreted as coming judgment
rationale: Jeremiah is told to hide stones before the Judeans' eyes, with their meaning stated in the next unit. The earlier command breaks a jar before accompanying men and explains it as the people's and city's breaking. The prophetic method is shared; the objects and predicted actions differ.
source_text: Take large stones for yourself and hide them in the forecourt at the gate of Pharaoh’s house at Taphnas, before the eyes of Judah’s men.

target_units.text: And smash the jar before the eyes of the men going out with you,
and say: Thus says the Lord: This is how I will smash this people and this city, as an earthenware vessel is smashed that cannot be healed again.

relationship: close prophecy that Nebuchadnezzar will receive Egypt
rationale: Jeremiah announces Nebuchadnezzar's arrival and throne above the hidden stones in Egypt. Ezekiel likewise names Nebuchadnezzar as the recipient of Egypt from God, there as wages for his force. The target does not mention Jeremiah's stones or throne-sign.
source_text: Say, Thus said the Lord: I am sending and will bring Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. He will place his throne above these stones that you hid and raise his weapons over them.

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord, the Lord: Behold, I give the land of Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. He will take her booty and strip her spoils; it will be wages for his force.
In exchange for his service, which he performed against Tyre, I have given him the land of Egypt. Thus says the Lord, the Lord:

relationship: close formula assigning people to death, sword or captivity
rationale: Both declarations distribute people to their appointed forms of judgment using the repeated construction those for a fate, to that fate. Jeremiah 15 includes famine as well; the source names death, deportation and sword in its Egyptian setting.
source_text: He will enter and strike Egypt’s land: those for death, to death; those for deportation, to deportation; and those for the sword, to the sword.

target_units.text: And if they say to you, ‘Where shall we go out?’ you will say to them: Thus says the Lord: As many as are for death, to death; as many for sword, to sword; as many for famine, to famine; as many for captivity, to captivity.

relationship: related judgment upon Egypt's gods in different historical settings
rationale: The source predicts burning the gods' houses and deporting the gods during the Babylonian attack. Exodus announces the Lord's vengeance upon Egypt's gods in the Passover setting. The agents, actions and occasions differ; both specifically include Egyptian deities within judgment.
source_text: He will kindle fire in the houses of their gods, burn the houses, and deport the gods. He will delouse Egypt’s land as a shepherd delouses his garment, and he will go out in peace.

target_units.text: I will go through the land of Egypt that night and strike every firstborn in the land of Egypt, both human and animal. Against all the Egyptians’ gods I will execute vengeance. I am the Lord.

relationship: related humiliation of deities carried into captivity
rationale: Jeremiah's oracle includes the deportation of Egypt's gods. Isaiah depicts the images of Bel and Dagon as burdens and says they themselves were led captive. This connection concerns divine images' captivity and does not identify those named images with the source's Egyptian gods or reinterpret its delousing simile.
source_text: He will kindle fire in the houses of their gods, burn the houses, and deport the gods. He will delouse Egypt’s land as a shepherd delouses his garment, and he will go out in peace.

target_units.text: Bel fell; Dagon was shattered. Their carved images became a burden for wild and domestic animals. Lift them, bound together, as a load for one who is weary
and hungry and exhausted, without strength at all; they cannot be saved from war, and they themselves were led captive.

relationship: related destruction of cultic pillars and shrines
rationale: Jeremiah predicts the shattering of the City of the Sun's pillars and burning of the houses. Exodus commands the breaking of pillars and destruction of other cultic objects in the land Israel is entering. This is a comparison of destructive treatment of rival cults, not an assertion that the commands describe the same place or army.
source_text: He will shatter the pillars of the City of the Sun, those in On, and burn their houses with fire.

target_units.text: Tear down their altars, break their pillars, cut down their sacred groves, and burn their gods’ carved images with fire.

relationship: related setting of Judean survivors in Egyptian Taphnas
rationale: The oracle addresses Judean communities in Egypt, including Taphnas. The preceding narrative records Johanan's party entering Egypt and reaching Taphnas. The target accounts for one stated destination without placing all the source's other communities there.
source_text: The word that came to Jeremiah for all the Judeans living in Egypt’s land and those staying at Migdol, Taphnas, and in Pathoures’s land:

target_units.text: They entered Egypt, for they had not obeyed the Lord’s voice. They entered Taphnas.

relationship: close recollection of Jerusalem's desolation after captivity
rationale: Jeremiah points to the devastation and emptied cities already visible in Judah. Lamentations opens with Israel taken captive, Jerusalem laid waste and the once populous city sitting alone. The lament specifically supports the Jerusalem portion of the source's wider judgment on Judah's cities.
source_text: Thus said the Lord, Israel’s God: You have seen all the calamities I brought upon Jerusalem and Judah’s cities. Behold, they are deserted of inhabitants,

target_units.text: After Israel was taken captive and Jerusalem laid waste, Jeremiah sat weeping and lamented this lament over Jerusalem, saying: How the city once full of peoples sat alone! She has become like a widow, she who was populous among the nations. A ruler among the regions has become subject to tribute.

relationship: close provocation through worship of previously unknown gods
rationale: The source attributes the calamity to provoking God by incense to other gods whom the people did not know. Deuteronomy speaks of provocation by foreign gods and sacrifice to gods they did not know. The forms of ritual action differ, while the unknown foreign recipients and divine provocation correspond.
source_text: because of the wickedness they committed to embitter Me, going to burn incense to other gods whom you did not know.

target_units.text: They provoked Me with foreign gods; with their abominations they embittered Me.
They sacrificed unto demons, and not unto God, unto gods whom they did not know; new ones, lately come, whom their fathers did not know.

relationship: close repeated sending of God's prophetic servants from dawn
rationale: Both passages describe God sending His servants the prophets at dawn. This source adds the particular prohibition of the hated act of defilement; the target places the repeated sending across the period since the exodus.
source_text: I sent you My servants the prophets at dawn, and I sent them saying, Do not commit this act of defilement that I hate.

target_units.text: From the day their fathers left Egypt’s land until this day, I sent out to you all My servants the prophets by day and at dawn, and I sent them.

relationship: parallel rejection of repeatedly sent divine messengers
rationale: Jeremiah says the people did not listen or turn from incense to other gods. Chronicles describes God's repeated sending of prophets and the people's disregard of His words and mockery of His messengers. The source specifies the ritual practice from which they refused to turn.
source_text: But they did not listen to Me or incline their ear to turn from their evils and stop burning incense to other gods.

target_units.text: The Lord, the God of their fathers, sent through prophets, rising early and sending His messengers, because He spared His people and His sanctuary.
They kept sneering at His messengers, treating His words as nothing, and mocking His prophets, until the Lord’s anger rose among His people, until there was no healing.

relationship: related divine wrath and destructive fire
rationale: Jeremiah says wrath dripped out and blazed in Judah's cities and outside Jerusalem. Lamentations describes poured-out fury and fire kindled in Zion consuming her foundations. The shared wrath-and-fire imagery connects the city's destruction with divine judgment.
source_text: My anger and wrath dripped out and blazed in Judah’s cities and outside Jerusalem, and they became a desolation and an untrodden place, as on this day.

target_units.text: The Lord completed His fury and poured out His furious anger. He kindled a fire in Zion, and it consumed her foundations.

relationship: close rhetorical charge that idolatrous provocation harms the people themselves
rationale: The source asks why the people do great evils against themselves, cutting off their households. The earlier oracle asks whether their provocative worship harms God or themselves to their shame. Both turn attention from the purported benefit of the cult to the worshipers' own harm.
source_text: Now thus said the Lord Almighty: Why are you doing great evils against yourselves, cutting off from yourselves man and woman, little child and nursing infant from Judah, so that none of you remains,

target_units.text: Is it Me they provoke to anger? says the Lord. Is it not themselves, so that their faces are put to shame?

relationship: close warning against provoking God through service to foreign gods
rationale: The source connects the works of their hands and incense to other gods with their own cutting off and reproach. Jeremiah 25 forbids service and worship of foreign gods so as not to provoke God through their hands' works into harming them. Neither comparison requires treating every mention of hands' works as an expressly described manufactured statue.
source_text: embittering Me with the work of your hands by burning incense to other gods in Egypt’s land, which you entered to live there, so that you are cut off and become a curse and a reproach among all the earth’s nations?

target_units.text: Do not follow foreign gods to serve them and bow down to them, so that you do not provoke Me by your hands’ works into harming you.

relationship: related warning not to repeat the fathers' evil
rationale: Jeremiah asks whether the earlier generations' and rulers' evils have been forgotten. Zechariah recalls God's anger with the fathers and forbids becoming like those who ignored calls to turn from evil. The source includes wives and rulers in addition to the fathers.
source_text: Have you forgotten your fathers’ evils, the evils of Judah’s kings, your rulers’ evils, and your wives’ evils, which they committed in Judah’s land and outside Jerusalem?

target_units.text: “The Lord was angry with your fathers with great anger.
You shall say to them: Thus says the Lord Almighty: Return to Me, and I will return to you, says the Lord.

Do not become like your fathers, against whom the former prophets brought charges, saying, ‘Thus says the Lord Almighty: Turn away from your evil ways and your evil practices.’ But they did not listen attentively to Me, says the Lord.

relationship: close failure to heed the ordinances given to the fathers
rationale: The source says the people have not stopped their practices or held fast to the ordinances set before the fathers. The earlier passage recalls the command to hear and walk in God's ways and the fathers' refusal. Both describe persistence in the opposite course to the received command.
source_text: They have not stopped to this day and have not held fast to My ordinances, which I set before their fathers.

target_units.text: But this utterance I commanded them, saying: Hear My voice, and I will be your God and you will be My people; and walk in all My ways that I command you, so that it may be well with you.
And they did not hear Me, and their ear did not attend, but they walked in the thoughts of their evil heart and went backward rather than forward.

relationship: related image of God setting His face in destructive judgment
rationale: The source states only that God is setting His face; its following unit supplies destruction of the Egyptian remnant. Leviticus explicitly sets God's face against a man and his kin in judgment. The connection concerns this image of divine opposition, not an identification of the different offenses.
source_text: Therefore thus said the Lord: I am setting My face

target_units.text: And I will set My face against that man and destroy him from among his people, because he gave some of his seed to a ruler, defiling My holy things and profaning the name of those consecrated to Me.
But if the natives of the land utterly overlook that man with their eyes, when he gives any of his seed unto a ruler, so as not to put him to death,
then I will set My face against that man and his kin. I will destroy him from among their people, together with all who agree with him so that he prostitutes himself after rulers.

relationship: close repetition of sword and famine against the Egyptian remnant
rationale: Both oracles locate the threatened people in Egypt and announce death by sword and famine. The source emphasizes the least and greatest and the resulting reproach and curse, while the earlier warning emphasizes the failure of the hoped-for escape.
source_text: to destroy all the survivors in Egypt, and they will fall. By sword and famine they will perish, from the least to the greatest, and become a reproach, a destruction, and a curse.

target_units.text: the sword you fear will find you in Egypt’s land, and the famine you are concerned about will catch up with you from behind in Egypt, and there you will die.
All the people and all the foreigners who set their faces toward Egypt’s land to live there will perish by sword and famine. None of them will be saved from the calamities I am bringing upon them.

relationship: close parallel between judgment in Egypt and prior judgment in Jerusalem
rationale: The source expressly says Egypt's residents will be visited as Jerusalem was. The earlier warning likewise compares wrath on those entering Egypt with wrath already falling on Jerusalem. Their lists of the judgment's effects differ.
source_text: I will visit those staying in Egypt’s land as I visited Jerusalem, by sword, famine, and death.

target_units.text: For thus said the Lord: As My wrath dripped upon Jerusalem’s inhabitants, so My wrath will drip upon you when you enter Egypt. You will become an untrodden place, subject to others, a curse, and a reproach, and you certainly will never see this place again.

relationship: same-chapter clarification of the exception for rescued returnees
rationale: The source denies return to Judah except for those rescued. The later statement identifies sword survivors who return, few in number. This clarifies the expressly stated exception rather than changing the warning into a promise of universal return.
source_text: None of Judah’s remainder residing in Egypt’s land will be saved to return to Judah’s land, where they hope in their souls to return. They certainly will not return except those rescued.

target_units.text: Those saved from the sword will return to Judah’s land, few in number. Judah’s survivors who settled in Egypt’s land to live there will know whose word will endure.

relationship: same-chapter link between men's knowledge and the women's appeal to their husbands
rationale: The source identifies men who knew of their wives' incense alongside the answering women. The women's later question asks whether they made cakes and poured offerings without their husbands. These statements connect the household participants without making mere knowledge identical to each person's performance of every ritual.
source_text: All the men who knew that their wives burned incense to other gods, all the women, a great assembly, and all the people staying in Egypt’s land at Pathoures answered Jeremiah:

target_units.text: And when we burn incense to the queen of heaven and poured out drink offerings to her, did we make cakes for her and pour out drink offerings to her without our husbands?

relationship: close explicit refusal to hear the divine warning
rationale: The people directly refuse to listen to Jeremiah's word in the Lord's name. In the earlier oracle they likewise answer the call to hear the watchers' trumpet by saying they will not hear. Both record an open verbal refusal rather than inadvertent failure to understand.
source_text: As for the word you spoke to us in the Lord’s name, we will not listen to you.

target_units.text: I have appointed watchers over you: Hear the trumpet’s sound! And they said, ‘We will not hear.’

relationship: related false attribution of material well-being to rival objects of devotion
rationale: The speakers credit devotion to the queen of heaven with bread and prosperity. Hosea's woman credits her lovers with provisions, while God says He gave the grain, wine and oil that she failed to recognize. The rival recipients differ; the comparison does not identify the queen of heaven with Baal or the lovers.
source_text: We will certainly do everything that will come from our mouths: burn incense to the queen of heaven and pour out drink offerings to her, as we, our fathers, our kings, and our rulers did in Judah’s cities and outside Jerusalem. We were filled with bread, were well off, and saw no calamities.

target_units.text: For their mother prostituted herself; she who bore them brought shame. She said, ‘I will follow my lovers, who give me my loaves and water, my garments and linen cloths, my oil and everything due to me.’
Therefore look, I block her way with thorns and will build up her roads, and she will certainly not find her path.

She will pursue her lovers but certainly not catch them; she will seek them but certainly not find them. She will say, ‘I will go and return to my former husband, for it was better for me then than now.’
She did not know that it was I who gave her grain, wine and oil and multiplied silver for her; but she made silver and gold objects for Baal.

relationship: contrast between rival explanations of lost provision
rationale: The people claim that stopping incense to the queen caused scarcity, sword and famine. Hosea identifies God as the provider who takes back His grain and wine. The target supplies a contrasting account of deprivation, while Jeremiah's subsequent reply likewise rejects the speakers' defense of their cult.
source_text: But when we stopped burning incense to the queen of heaven, we were all diminished and perished by sword and famine.

target_units.text: She did not know that it was I who gave her grain, wine and oil and multiplied silver for her; but she made silver and gold objects for Baal.
Therefore I will return and recover My grain at its season and My wine at its time; I will take away My garments and linen cloths so that they do not cover her shame.

relationship: close household involvement in cakes and drink offerings to heavenly recipients
rationale: The women mention making cakes and pouring drink offerings and question whether this was without their husbands. The earlier oracle describes children, fathers and women preparing cakes for heaven's host and pouring offerings to foreign gods. The source says queen of heaven, whereas the target says heaven's host; the recipients' terms are not made identical.
source_text: And when we burn incense to the queen of heaven and poured out drink offerings to her, did we make cakes for her and pour out drink offerings to her without our husbands?

target_units.text: Their sons gather wood, and their fathers burn a fire, and their women work dough to make cakes for heaven’s host; and they poured drink offerings to foreign gods to provoke Me to anger.

relationship: related divine remembrance of cultic wrongdoing for judgment
rationale: Jeremiah says the people's earlier incense came into God's heart and remembrance. Hosea says God does not accept the sacrifices and will remember injustices and punish sins. Both oppose a favorable reading of ritual conduct by invoking God's adverse remembrance.
source_text: Was it not the incense you burned in Judah’s cities and outside Jerusalem—you, your fathers, your kings, your rulers, and the people of the land—that the Lord remembered, and did it not come into His heart?

target_units.text: Because even if they offer a sacrifice and eat meat, the Lord will not accept them. Now He will remember their injustices and punish their sins. They returned to Egypt and will eat unclean things among the Assyrians.

relationship: close correspondence between covenant curses and the desolate land
rationale: Jeremiah explains the land's desolation and curse by unbearable wickedness and abominations. Leviticus threatens desolate cities and land, ruined holy places and scattering among nations for covenant disobedience. The source describes the resulting condition; the target states the threatened consequences.
source_text: The Lord could no longer bear the wickedness of your actions and the abominations you had committed. Your land became a desolation, an untrodden place, and a curse, as on this day,

target_units.text: and I will make your cities desolate, and lay waste your holy places; and I will in no wise smell the savour of your sacrifices;
and I Myself will desolate your land, and your enemies who dwell in it shall marvel at it.
And I will scatter you among the nations, and the advancing sword shall consume you. Your land shall become desolate, and your cities shall be desolate.

relationship: close causal link between refusing God's voice and overtaking calamities
rationale: The source attributes the calamities to failing to obey God's voice and walk in His ordinances, law and testimonies. Deuteronomy says curses will come and overtake those who do not hear the Lord's voice and keep His commandments. The source also specifies the incense that occasioned the charge.
source_text: because you burned incense, sinned against the Lord, did not obey the Lord’s voice, and did not walk in His ordinances, law, and testimonies. These calamities have seized you.

target_units.text: And it shall be, if you do not hearken unto the voice of the Lord your God, to keep and do all His commandments which I command you this day, that all these curses shall come upon you, and overtake you.

relationship: contrast between fulfillment of idolatrous pledges and vows made to God
rationale: The source says the women carried out their pledges to the queen of heaven. Ecclesiastes requires paying vows made to God and warns against vowing without paying. The comparison concerns the seriousness of enacted pledges while distinguishing their recipients; it does not commend the women's idolatrous vows.
source_text: Thus said the Lord, Israel’s God: You women spoke with your mouths and fulfilled it with your hands, saying, We will certainly carry out our pledges that we pledged, to burn incense to the queen of heaven and pour out drink offerings to her. You firmly persisted in your pledges and indeed carried them out.

target_units.text: Whenever you vow a vow to God, do not delay paying it, for there is no delight in fools. Pay whatever you vow.
Better that you do not vow than that you vow and do not pay.

relationship: related withholding of the Lord's name amid judgment
rationale: The source announces that Judeans in Egypt will no longer invoke the living Lord's name. In Amos, amid deaths in a house, one person tells another to be silent so as not to name the Lord. The source is God's sworn declaration; the target records a human warning, not that identical oath.
source_text: Therefore hear the Lord’s word, all Judah staying in Egypt’s land: I have sworn by My great name, said the Lord, that My name will no longer be in any Judean’s mouth to say, As the Lord, the Lord, lives, throughout Egypt’s land.

target_units.text: Their relatives will take them and force their way to bring their bones out of the house. He will say to those in charge of the house, “Is there anyone else with you?” He will say, “No more.” Then he will say, “Be silent, so as not to name the Lord’s name.”

relationship: related divine oath by God's own authority
rationale: God swears by His great name in the source. Hebrews says God swore by Himself because there was no greater by whom to swear. The oath in Hebrews confirms blessing to Abraham, while Jeremiah's oath announces judgment.
source_text: Therefore hear the Lord’s word, all Judah staying in Egypt’s land: I have sworn by My great name, said the Lord, that My name will no longer be in any Judean’s mouth to say, As the Lord, the Lord, lives, throughout Egypt’s land.

target_units.text: For when God made a promise to Abraham, since He had no one greater by whom to swear, He swore by Himself,

relationship: close divine attention directed toward harm rather than good
rationale: Jeremiah says God watches the people for harm, not good, and announces sword and famine. Amos says God will fix His eyes on the captives for evils, not good things, and command the sword against them. The correspondence concerns purposeful divine attention in judgment.
source_text: For I am watching over them to harm them, not do them good. All Judah living in Egypt’s land will perish by sword and famine until they perish.

target_units.text: If they go into captivity before their enemies, I will command the sword there, and it will kill them. I will fix My eyes upon them for evils and not for good things.”

relationship: related testing of disputed words by their eventual outcome
rationale: The few returnees will learn whose word endures, after rival claims about safety and prosperity. Deuteronomy judges a claimed divine word by whether it comes to pass. The source's disputed speakers are not all described as prophets, whereas the law addresses prophetic claims explicitly.
source_text: Those saved from the sword will return to Judah’s land, few in number. Judah’s survivors who settled in Egypt’s land to live there will know whose word will endure.

target_units.text: And if you say in your heart: How shall we know the word which the Lord has not spoken?

Whatsoever the prophet speaks in the name of the Lord, if the word does not come to pass, nor is fulfilled, that is the word which the Lord has not spoken. That prophet has spoken in ungodliness; you shall not spare him.

relationship: close narrative counterpart to the stated Zedekiah comparison
rationale: The threat against Egypt's Ouaphre is compared with God's handover of Zedekiah to Nebuchadnezzar. The closing narrative records Zedekiah's capture and removal to Babylon. It supports the named comparison, without supplying a narrated fulfillment of Ouaphre's fate.
source_text: Thus said the Lord: I am handing Ouaphre king of Egypt over to his enemy and those seeking his life, as I handed Zedekiah king of Judah over to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, his enemy who sought his life.

target_units.text: and the Chaldean force pursued the king and overtook him beyond Jericho. All his servants scattered away from him.
They captured the king and brought him to the king of Babylon at Deblatha, and he spoke to him in judgment.
The king of Babylon slaughtered Zedekiah’s sons before his eyes, and he slaughtered all Judah’s rulers at Deblatha.
He blinded Zedekiah’s eyes and bound him in fetters. The king of Babylon brought him to Babylon and put him in a mill house until the day he died.

relationship: close corroborating notice of Baruch's writing in Jehoiakim's fourth year
rationale: Both accounts place Baruch's writing from Jeremiah's mouth in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah. The earlier narrative describes the commission and act; this source introduces the personal word addressed to the writer.
source_text: The word Jeremiah the prophet spoke to Baruch son of Neriah when he wrote these words in the scroll from Jeremiah’s mouth, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah king of Judah:

target_units.text: In the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, the Lord’s word came to me:

Take a writing roll and write on it all the words I have delivered to you as oracles concerning Jerusalem, Judah, and all the nations, from the day I spoke to you, from the days of Josiah king of Judah until today.
Perhaps Judah’s house will hear all the calamities I intend to bring upon them, so that they turn from their evil way and I may be merciful toward their injustices and sins.
Jeremiah called Baruch son of Neriah, and he wrote on a writing roll, from Jeremiah’s mouth, all the Lord’s words which He had delivered to him as oracles.

relationship: close lament of weary groaning at one's resting place
rationale: Baruch says he lay amid groanings and found no rest after toil was added to pain. The psalm speaks of weariness with groaning and tears wetting the bed and resting place. It supplies a comparable bodily lament, not Baruch's identity or the same occasion.
source_text: For you said, Woe to me, woe to me! The Lord has added toil to my pain. I lay down amid groanings and found no rest.

target_units.text: I grew weary with my groaning; every night I will bathe my bed, with my tears I will wet my resting place.

relationship: close opposing images of uprooting or demolishing and building or planting
rationale: God announces tearing down what He built and plucking up what He planted. Jeremiah's commission similarly includes uprooting and demolishing alongside building and planting. The source describes reversal of prior constructive work, while the commission lists the prophet's appointed scope.
source_text: Tell him, Thus said the Lord: Those I have built up I am tearing down, and those I have planted I am plucking up.

target_units.text: Behold, today I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms, to uproot, demolish, destroy, build and plant.

relationship: close personal assurance that one's life will be gain amid calamity
rationale: Baruch is promised his life as gain wherever he goes while calamity comes upon all flesh. Ebed-melech likewise receives a promise that his life will be his gain. Their immediate grounds differ: Baruch is warned against seeking great things, while Ebed-melech is commended for trust.
source_text: Are you seeking great things for yourself? Do not seek them, for I am bringing calamities upon all flesh, says the Lord. I will give your life as gain wherever you walk.

target_units.text: I will certainly save you. You certainly will not fall by the sword; your life will be your gain because you trusted in Me, says the Lord.

relationship: parallel refusal to pursue great things for oneself
rationale: The source forbids Baruch to seek great things for himself amid general calamity. The psalm says the speaker's heart and eyes are not exalted and that he has not walked among great things beyond him. This target supports the restraint of ambition, distinct from the source's promise of preserved life.
source_text: Are you seeking great things for yourself? Do not seek them, for I am bringing calamities upon all flesh, says the Lord. I will give your life as gain wherever you walk.

target_units.text: A song of the ascents. For David. Lord, my heart was not exalted, nor were my eyes raised high; I did not walk among great things nor among wonders beyond me.

relationship: close parallel age and length of Zedekiah's reign
rationale: Both accounts state that Zedekiah began to reign at twenty-one and reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. The source additionally names his mother and adds Lobena, details which this target does not provide.
source_text: Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Amitaal daughter of Jeremiah, from Lobena.

target_units.text: Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem.

relationship: close parallel regnal notice including the king's mother
rationale: Both notices give the age twenty-one and eleven years in Jerusalem and name the mother as a daughter of Jeremiah. The source says Zedekiah and Amitaal and adds Lobena; Kings says Sedekias and Amital and does not name Lobena in this unit.
source_text: Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Amitaal daughter of Jeremiah, from Lobena.

target_units.text: Sedekias was twenty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Amital daughter of Jeremiah.

relationship: close parallel commencement of the Babylonian siege
rationale: Both place the Babylonian king's arrival with his force in the ninth regnal year and tenth month and describe surrounding siegeworks. Jeremiah adds the tenth day and specifies a palisade and squared stones; Kings describes an enclosing wall.
source_text: In the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, on the tenth of the month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and all his force came against Jerusalem. They enclosed her with a palisade and built around her with squared stones.

target_units.text: In the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, Nabouchodonosor king of Babylon came with all his force against Jerusalem. He camped against it and built an enclosing wall against it all around.

relationship: close parallel endpoint of the siege
rationale: Both accounts say the city remained besieged until the king's eleventh year, naming him Zedekiah in Jeremiah and Sedekias in Kings. Neither comparison changes the supplied chronology or name forms.
source_text: The city was under siege until the eleventh year of King Zedekiah.

target_units.text: The city remained under siege until King Sedekias’s eleventh year.

relationship: close parallel report of famine and absence of bread
rationale: Both accounts place severe famine on the ninth of the month and say there were no loaves for the people of the land. The individual units do not themselves supply the month's number.
source_text: On the ninth of the month, the famine grew severe in the city, and there were no loaves for the people of the land.

target_units.text: On the ninth of the month the famine grew severe in the city, and there were no loaves for the people of the land.

relationship: close parallel escape route after Jerusalem's breach
rationale: Both describe the breach, warriors going out at night by the gate between walls beside the king's garden, the surrounding Chaldeans and the route toward Arabah or Araba. The detailed cluster supports a close narrative comparison without normalizing the place-name forms.
source_text: The city was breached, and all the warriors went out at night by the gate between the wall and the outer wall beside the king’s garden, while the Chaldeans surrounded the city. They went by the road to Arabah,

target_units.text: The city was breached, and all the men of war went out by night by way of the gate between the walls, the one belonging to the king’s garden, with the Chaldeans surrounding the city. He went by the way of the Araba.

relationship: close parallel pursuit and capture near Jericho
rationale: Both describe the Chaldean pursuit overtaking the king near Jericho and the dispersal of those with him. Jeremiah calls them his servants; Kings calls them his force. The corresponding movement is shared without making those designations identical.
source_text: and the Chaldean force pursued the king and overtook him beyond Jericho. All his servants scattered away from him.

target_units.text: The Chaldean force pursued the king and overtook him in Araboth Jericho, and all his force scattered away from him.

relationship: close parallel royal judgment at Deblatha
rationale: Both accounts bring the captured king to Babylon's king at Deblatha and describe judgment being spoken upon him. The named place and judicial encounter provide a specific counterpart.
source_text: They captured the king and brought him to the king of Babylon at Deblatha, and he spoke to him in judgment.

target_units.text: They seized the king and brought him to the king of Babylon at Deblatha, and he pronounced judgment upon him.

relationship: close parallel killing of the king's sons before his eyes
rationale: Both accounts explicitly put the sons' slaughter before the father's eyes. Jeremiah additionally reports the killing of Judah's rulers at Deblatha; Kings proceeds to the king's blinding and fetters.
source_text: The king of Babylon slaughtered Zedekiah’s sons before his eyes, and he slaughtered all Judah’s rulers at Deblatha.

target_units.text: He slaughtered Sedekias’s sons before his eyes. He blinded Sedekias’s eyes, bound him with fetters, and brought him to Babylon.

relationship: close parallel blinding, fetters and deportation of the king
rationale: Both accounts describe the king being blinded, bound with fetters and brought to Babylon. Jeremiah additionally places him in a mill house until death; that detail is not replaced with a conventional prison description or attributed to Kings.
source_text: He blinded Zedekiah’s eyes and bound him in fetters. The king of Babylon brought him to Babylon and put him in a mill house until the day he died.

target_units.text: He slaughtered Sedekias’s sons before his eyes. He blinded Sedekias’s eyes, bound him with fetters, and brought him to Babylon.

relationship: related prediction of arrival in Babylon without seeing it
rationale: Jeremiah's blinded king is brought to Babylon. Ezekiel predicts that Jerusalem's ruler will be caught, brought to Babylon and not see it, and die there. The narrative supplies a particular counterpart to arrival without sight; Ezekiel does not name Zedekiah in the target unit.
source_text: He blinded Zedekiah’s eyes and bound him in fetters. The king of Babylon brought him to Babylon and put him in a mill house until the day he died.

target_units.text: I will spread My net over him, and he will be caught in My enclosure. I will bring him to Babylon, to the Chaldeans’ land, and he will not see it, and there he will die.

relationship: close parallel arrival of the Babylonian officer with a differing day
rationale: Both accounts place the officer's arrival at Jerusalem in the fifth month. Jeremiah gives the tenth day and calls him chief guard; Kings gives the seventh day, the nineteenth year of the Babylonian king, and the title chief cook. The differing details remain explicit.
source_text: In the fifth month, on the tenth of the month, Nebuzaradan, the chief guard who stood before the king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem.

target_units.text: In the fifth month, on the seventh of the month, in the nineteenth year of Nabouchodonosor king of Babylon, Nabouzardan, the chief cook who stood before the king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem.
