relationship: close parallel burning of the sanctuary, palace and city houses
rationale: Both accounts name the Lord's house, the king's house and Jerusalem's houses as burned. The target's final agent phrase continues into verse10, so both actual units are retained together as one passage.
source_text: He burned the Lord’s house, the king’s house, and all the city’s houses; every great house he burned with fire.

target_units.text: He set fire to the Lord’s house, the king’s house, and all Jerusalem’s houses; every house was set ablaze by
the chief cook.

relationship: close parallel demolition of Jerusalem's wall
rationale: Jeremiah records the Chaldean force pulling down Jerusalem's wall all around. Chronicles likewise says the wall was demolished amid the burning of the sanctuary and citadels. This target expressly contains wall demolition, unlike the supplied 2 Kings 25:10 wording.
source_text: The Chaldean force with the chief guard pulled down the whole wall of Jerusalem all around.

target_units.text: He burned the Lord’s house, demolished Jerusalem’s wall, and burned its citadels with fire, consigning every beautiful article to destruction.

relationship: close parallel retention of people as vinedressers
rationale: Both accounts say the Babylonian officer left people as vinedressers. Jeremiah adds farmers; Kings calls the remaining people poor and adds the native term gabin. The comparison does not silently translate that latter term as the source's farmers.
source_text: The chief guard left the remaining people as vinedressers and farmers.

target_units.text: The chief cook left some of the land’s poor as vinedressers and as gabin.

relationship: close parallel removal of bronze temple fixtures to Babylon
rationale: Both accounts describe Chaldeans shattering the bronze pillars and Sea and carrying their bronze to Babylon. Jeremiah names bases, whereas Kings retains mechonoth. The shared named fixtures and destination are explicit without replacing that native term.
source_text: The Chaldeans shattered the bronze pillars in the Lord’s house, the bases, and the bronze Sea in the Lord’s house. They took their bronze and carried it to Babylon.

target_units.text: The Chaldeans shattered the bronze pillars in the Lord’s house, the mechonoth, and the bronze sea in the Lord’s house, and carried their bronze to Babylon.

relationship: parallel inventories of bronze service utensils with differing item lists
rationale: Both passages enumerate bronze objects used in service, including bowls. Jeremiah also names the rim and meat forks; Kings names cauldrons, iamin and incense dishes. The inventories are related without treating all the supplied item names as interchangeable.
source_text: And the rim, the bowls, the meat forks, and all the bronze utensils with which they performed service,

target_units.text: He took the cauldrons, the iamin, the bowls, the incense dishes, and all the bronze utensils with which they ministered.

relationship: close parallel taking of gold and silver temple vessels
rationale: Jeremiah distinguishes the gold and silver objects taken by the chief guard within a broader utensil list. Kings records the chief cook taking firepans and gold and silver bowls. This supports the precious-metal spoliation without supplying glosses for saphphoth or masmaroth.
source_text: and the saphphoth, the masmaroth, the pouring vessels, the lampstands, the incense bowls, and the ladles—those of gold, gold, and those of silver, silver—the chief guard took.

target_units.text: The chief cook took the firepans and the gold and silver bowls,

relationship: close parallel unweighed bronze of Solomon's temple furnishings
rationale: Both accounts name Solomon, two pillars, one Sea and bronze beyond a reckoned weight. Jeremiah includes twelve calves beneath the Sea, while Kings includes mechonoth. Their lists are not made identical.
source_text: The two pillars, the one Sea, and the twelve bronze calves beneath the Sea, which King Solomon made for the Lord’s house—their bronze was beyond weighing.

target_units.text: the two pillars, the one sea, and the mechonoth which Solomon made for the Lord’s house. The bronze of all the objects had no reckoned weight.

relationship: close counterpart for twelve animals supporting the Sea
rationale: Jeremiah names twelve bronze calves beneath the Sea. Kings describes twelve cattle beneath it, grouped three in each of four directions, with the Sea above them. This target specifically supports the supporting-animal arrangement rather than the separate unweighed-bronze statement.
source_text: The two pillars, the one Sea, and the twelve bronze calves beneath the Sea, which King Solomon made for the Lord’s house—their bronze was beyond weighing.

target_units.text: Twelve cattle were beneath the Sea: three facing north, three facing the sea, three facing south, and three facing east. All their hindquarters faced the house, and the Sea was above them.

relationship: parallel descriptions of a temple pillar with differing heights
rationale: Jeremiah assigns one pillar a height of thirty-five cubits; Kings gives one pillar eighteen cubits. Both describe the same class of temple furnishing, but the measurements are expressly different and are not reconciled by the comparison.
source_text: As for the pillars, one pillar was thirty-five cubits high, and a cord of twelve cubits encircled it. Its thickness was four fingerbreadths all around,

target_units.text: One pillar was eighteen cubits high, with the bronze chothar upon it. The chothar was three cubits high, with sabacha and pomegranates around the chothar, all bronze. The second pillar was the same, with the sabacha.

relationship: related thirty-five-cubit pillar description with different grammatical scope
rationale: Jeremiah describes one pillar as thirty-five cubits high. Chronicles describes two pillars before the house as thirty-five cubits in height. The shared measurement language is noted without deciding whether the latter expression measures each pillar or combines them.
source_text: As for the pillars, one pillar was thirty-five cubits high, and a cord of twelve cubits encircled it. Its thickness was four fingerbreadths all around,

target_units.text: He made two pillars before the house, thirty-five cubits in height, and their capitals five cubits.

relationship: close correspondence of pillar ornaments, nets and pomegranates
rationale: Jeremiah describes bronze cornices surrounded by netting and pomegranates. Kings lists pillar ornaments covered by nets and rows of pomegranates. The differing ornament terminology and the target's four-hundred enumeration are preserved rather than made identical to Jeremiah's count.
source_text: and a bronze cornice was on them. The projection of one cornice was five cubits in length, and a net and pomegranates surrounded the cornice, all of bronze. The second pillar had the same: eight pomegranates per cubit over the twelve cubits.

target_units.text: two pillars, the two twisted ornaments of the pillars on top of the pillars, and the two nets covering both twisted ornaments of the carvings on the pillars;
four hundred pomegranates for both nets, two rows of pomegranates for each net, covering both twisted ornaments on both pillars;

relationship: related hundred-pomegranate enumeration with differing descriptions
rationale: Jeremiah counts ninety-six on one side and one hundred around the net. Chronicles says a hundred pomegranates were made and placed on hanging ornaments. The passages share a numbered pomegranate decoration but do not explain how their arrangements and counting scopes correspond.
source_text: There were ninety-six pomegranates on one side; all the pomegranates around the net numbered one hundred.

target_units.text: He made serseroth in the dabir and placed them upon the pillars’ capitals. He made a hundred pomegranates and placed them upon the hanging ornaments.

relationship: parallel seizure of priestly personnel and three guards with different identifications
rationale: Both accounts include a first priest and three guards in the seized group. Jeremiah leaves the priests unnamed and calls the guards men guarding the road; Kings names Saraias and Sophonias and calls the three doorpost guards. The comparison does not identify the unnamed second priest with a named person or erase the different guard descriptions.
source_text: The chief guard took the first priest, the second priest, and the three men guarding the road,

target_units.text: The chief cook took Saraias the first priest, Sophonias, son of the second rank, and the three doorpost guards,

relationship: close parallel captive officials with a differing court-party count
rationale: Both lists include a eunuch supervising warriors, a military scribe and sixty people found in the city. Jeremiah gives seven prominent men in the king's presence; Kings gives five who saw his face. That numerical difference is retained.
source_text: and one eunuch who supervised the warriors, seven prominent men in the king’s presence who were found in the city, the scribe of the forces who kept records for the people of the land, and sixty people from the people of the land found inside the city.

target_units.text: and from the city he took one eunuch who supervised the warriors, five men who saw the king’s face who were found in the city, the scribe of the commander of the force who drew up the people of the land, and sixty men of the people of the land found in the city.

relationship: close parallel transfer of captives to Babylon's king at Deblatha
rationale: Both accounts describe the Babylonian officer taking the detained group to the king at Deblatha. Their supplied officer titles differ, chief guard in Jeremiah and chief cook in Kings.
source_text: Nebuzaradan, the chief guard, took them and brought them to the king of Babylon at Deblatha,

target_units.text: Nabouzardan, the chief cook, took them and led them to the king of Babylon at Deblatha.

relationship: close parallel royal violence at Deblatha in Aimath
rationale: Both accounts say Babylon's king struck the captives at Deblatha in Aimath's land. Kings explicitly adds that he put them to death and that Judah was deported; the source's shorter wording is preserved.
source_text: and the king of Babylon struck them at Deblatha in Aimath’s land.

target_units.text: The king of Babylon struck them and put them to death at Deblatha in Aimath’s land. Judah was deported from its land.

relationship: close parallel royal release with differing day and name forms
rationale: Both date a Judean king's release to the thirty-seventh year of deportation and the twelfth month. Jeremiah names Ioakim and gives the twenty-fourth day; Kings names Joakim and gives the twenty-seventh. The close sequence is compared without harmonizing those details or supplying a different Judean royal name.
source_text: In the thirty-seventh year after Ioakim king of Judah had been deported, in the twelfth month, on the twenty-fourth of the month, Oulaimaradach king of Babylon, in the year he became king, took up the head of Ioakim king of Judah and brought him out of the house where he was guarded.

target_units.text: In the thirty-seventh year of the deportation of Joakim king of Judah, in the twelfth month, on the twenty-seventh of the month, Euilmarodach king of Babylon, in the year of his reign, lifted the head of Joakim king of Judah and brought him out of his prison house.

relationship: close parallel kind speech and elevation above other kings
rationale: Both passages describe kind speech to the Judean king and placement of his throne above those of the other kings in Babylon. The distinct supplied names in their preceding units remain as written.
source_text: He spoke kindly to him and placed his throne above the thrones of the kings with him in Babylon.

target_units.text: He spoke kindly to him and placed his throne above the thrones of the kings who were with him in Babylon,

relationship: close parallel change of prison clothing and continual royal meals
rationale: Both accounts describe changing prison garments and eating bread continually before the Babylonian king throughout life. The clothing and daily-table details form a specific verbal and narrative correspondence.
source_text: He changed his prison robe, and he ate bread continually before him all the days he lived.

target_units.text: and he changed his prison garments, and he ate bread continually before him all the days of his life.

relationship: close parallel daily royal allowance for life
rationale: Both accounts give continual provision from the Babylonian royal establishment, apportioned day by day for the rest of the Judean king's life. Jeremiah calls it an allowance and expressly says until death; Kings describes table provision and each day's portion.
source_text: His allowance was given to him continually by the king of Babylon, from day to day until the day he died.

target_units.text: His table provision was given to him continually from the king’s house, each day’s portion on its day, all the days of his life.
